She kept them in a box. When she died, we found hundreds. She had written to people who were already dead, sometimes. She didn't care. The writing was the point.

My grandfather, her husband, kept a notebook. Not a journal—he hated that word, too self-conscious. Just a notebook where he wrote down things he noticed. "The way light hits the kitchen floor at 4pm in October." "Mrs. Patterson's cat, the orange one, finally caught a bird." Small observations, accumulated over forty years. When he died, we read them. It was like getting to know him again, but slower. More carefully.

I don't know what will happen to my drafts folder. Probably nothing. It'll get backed up to some cloud server, then forgotten, then eventually deleted by some automated process I won't understand. The messages will disappear without ever having been read by their intended recipients. Is that better or worse than sending them? I genuinely don't know.

There's a message to an ex that I've rewritten eleven times. It's about forgiveness, or maybe it's about blame. The lines blur. I wanted to say something true, but I also wanted to be understood, and those are different projects. Maybe they're incompatible. Maybe that's why I never sent it. Maybe I was protecting myself, or maybe I was protecting the version of her that exists in my head, the one who might read it and feel something, and then the real her would be disappointed by whatever I actually wrote.

I sent a message last week. It was simple. "Thinking of you." She wrote back an hour later. We talked for a while. It was good. It was also, I realized afterward, a kind of performance. We were both performing being okay, being connected, being people who had moved on. The message itself was fine. The context around it was a construction. We build these little theaters for each other, don't we? Small stages where we can be the people we wish we were.

My therapist says I intellectualize my feelings. I think she's right. I think I do it because feelings are heavy and words are light, and I like things I can hold up to the light and examine from different angles. But feelings don't work that way. They just sit there, in your chest, making it hard to breathe sometimes. You can't examine them. You can only carry them, or put them down, or let someone else help you carry them.

I'm trying to put some down. That's what this is, I guess. Practice. Writing without an audience, or with an audience of one who will never read it. The page doesn't judge. The page doesn't need anything from me. It just receives.

There's a message in my drafts to a friend who moved to another country. I started it the day she left. "I don't know how to—" and then nothing. I've tried to write it again so many times. But the not-knowing was the point, wasn't it? The not-knowing how to be her friend from far away. The not-knowing how to miss someone without making them feel guilty for leaving. The not-knowing how to want things for other people that they don't want for themselves.

She texts me sometimes. Short messages. "Saw a dog that looked like yours." "Ate something spicy and thought of you." We've built a language of small things. It's not the same as what we had. But it's something. It's a bridge, maybe, or a rope, or just a habit we're maintaining because stopping feels like admitting something.

I used to think that honesty was the highest virtue in relationships. Now I think it's more complicated. Sometimes honesty is a gift. Sometimes it's a weapon. Sometimes it's just noise, the sound of your own voice echoing in a room where no one asked you to speak. The drafts folder is where I put the honesty I'm not sure about. The honesty that might hurt. The honesty that might be misunderstood. The honesty that I'm not even sure is true, because feelings change, and by the time I finish a sentence, I might feel differently than when I started it.

There's a message to myself. I write these sometimes, when I can't sleep. "You are not behind." "You are not failing." "The thing you're afraid of is not as likely as you think." They don't work, not really. But they're something to do with my hands, with my mind, when the dark is too quiet and my thoughts start circling. The drafts folder holds these too. A conversation with myself that never quite ends.

I wonder if everyone has this. The hidden archive of almost-said things. The words that got caught in the throat. The love that was too big for its container and spilled over, leaving stains. I think we do. I think we carry these ghosts around, these unborn messages, and they shape us in ways we don't acknowledge. They make us more careful, or less careful. They make us brave in some areas and cowardly in others. They are, in their way, a kind of autobiography. The story of who we almost were, who we almost said we were, to the people who mattered.

I'm going to delete some of them. Not all. Some I want to keep, as evidence. As proof that I felt these things, intensely, even if I never expressed them properly. The rest—I'll let them go. They've served their purpose. They've been witnesses. Now they can be released.

Or maybe I'll keep them. Maybe I'll back them up, encrypt them, hide them somewhere only I can find. A time capsule of my almosts. For whoever I become, someday, to discover. To understand. To forgive, maybe, or to finally understand what I was afraid of.

The cursor blinks. Waiting. I could write more. I probably will, eventually. There's always more. There's always the next thing to almost say, the next feeling to almost name, the next love to almost give away.

But for now, I'll stop here. I'll leave this unsent, too. A message to no one, about the difficulty of messages, about the weight of words we carry and the words we release. About the strange mercy of the drafts folder, where nothing is final, where everything is still possible, where we can be brave and cowardly at the same time, where we can practice being the people we're trying to become.

Goodnight, drafts folder. Goodnight, almosts. Goodnight, all of us, writing in the dark, hoping someone will someday read what we couldn't send.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The Weight of Small Things

I keep thinking about the way my grandmother peeled an apple. One continuous spiral, the knife never leaving the fruit, the peel falling onto the newspaper she'd spread across the kitchen table. She did this every morning for my grandfather, who had diabetes and shouldn't have been eating apples at all, but he loved them, and she loved him, and so there was the apple, there was the spiral, there was the small rebellion of sweetness in a house full of careful measuring.

I was seven when I tried to do it myself. The peel broke. I cried. She didn't laugh, which I appreciated. She just took the knife and finished it, and then she let me try again with a pear, which is more forgiving, which has thinner skin, which taught me that some things are easier to learn than others.

She died in winter. I remember because the hospice nurse kept adjusting the thermostat and my mother kept adjusting it back, and they never spoke about it, this small war over degrees, over who got to decide what comfort meant. I was twenty-three. I had just started graduate school. I had just learned that my boyfriend was leaving me for someone in his program, someone who understood his work in a way I never would. I came home from the funeral and found the pear tree in my parents' backyard still holding a few fruits, brown and soft, nobody had thought to pick them.

I picked them. I made a crumble. I ate it standing at the sink, wearing my grandfather's old cardigan, which smelled like him still, like the pipe tobacco he'd quit smoking thirty years before but which somehow remained in the wool, in the closet, in the house itself.

---

There's a theory that we are all haunted. Not by ghosts, exactly, but by the versions of ourselves we used to be. The child who believed in Santa Claus. The teenager who thought heartbreak would kill her. The young adult who was certain she would change the world. These selves don't disappear. They accumulate. They sit in the back of the mind like passengers on a long train ride, occasionally leaning forward to say something, to remind you of who you were, of what you wanted, of what you lost.

I think about this when I see my students. They are so certain, so urgent, so convinced that their current crisis is the only crisis that has ever mattered. I want to tell them it gets better, but I also know that's a lie. It doesn't get better. It gets different. The crises change shape. They become quieter, more internal, less dramatic but somehow more persistent. The heartbreak doesn't kill you, but it leaves a scar. The ambition doesn't disappear, but it learns to coexist with doubt. The certainty evaporates, and in its place comes something more complicated, more honest, more useful.

I had a student last year who wrote an essay about her grandmother's hands. She described them as "map-like," full of routes and destinations and places she'd been. I gave it an A, but I wanted to give it something more. I wanted to tell her that her grandmother's hands were also young once, smooth and unmarked, that the map was written over time, that every line was a story, that she was lucky to have known the hands in their later form, when they had so much to say.

She came to office hours. She was worried about her GPA, about grad school applications, about whether she should take the job in Seattle or wait for something better. I told her about my grandmother's apple. I told her about the broken peel, the pear, the winter, the crumble eaten at the sink. She looked at me like I was speaking a foreign language. Maybe I was. Maybe that's what happens when you get older. You start speaking in stories, in metaphors, in the indirect language of people who have learned that directness rarely works, that the truth is better approached from an angle, that sometimes the most important things are the ones you almost don't say.

---

I walked past a bookstore today and saw a display of new releases. So many books. So many voices, so many attempts to make sense of the world, to capture something true, to be heard. I used to want to write a book. I still do, sometimes, in the small hours when I can't sleep and the house is quiet and I can hear my own breathing like a tide coming in and going out. But I also know now that wanting is not the same as doing. That the gap between intention and action is where most of us live, where we spend our lives, making small movements toward something we may never reach.

My mother calls every Sunday. She is eighty-two. She has started to forget things—names, appointments, the reason she walked into a room. But she remembers the apple story. She remembers the pear tree. She remembers the cardigan, the crumble, the way I stood at her sink in my grandfather's sweater and ate something sweet in a house that was already changing, already becoming the place where he would die, where she would live alone, where I would visit and try to be helpful and mostly just be present, which is its own kind of help, its own kind of love.

After we hang up, I sit with the phone in my hand. I think about all the things I didn't say. The questions I didn't ask. The silences that passed between us, comfortable and uncomfortable both, the silences of people who have known each other so long they no longer need to fill every space with words. I think about how love works this way. How it becomes a practice, a habit, a series of small attentions that accumulate into something larger than any single moment, any single conversation, any single Sunday phone call.

---

The light is changing as I write this. It's late afternoon, the time when the sun comes through the west windows and turns everything gold, temporary, precious. I think about my students again. About the essay. About the hands, map-like, full of stories. I think about my grandmother's spiral peel, unbroken, perfect, the knife moving in a circle that never ended, that could never end, that was always in the process of becoming.

I don't know what I'm trying to say. I think that's the point. Some things don't need to be said. They need to be witnessed. They need to be held in the mind like light, like warmth, like the particular quality of attention we bring to the world when we are paying attention, when we are awake, when we are here, in this moment, in this room, with these words that will disappear as soon as I stop writing them, that will remain only in the memory of having written, of having tried, of having reached toward something I may never fully grasp.

The sun is lower now. The gold is fading. I should probably make dinner. I should probably call my mother back, ask her what she had for lunch, tell her I love her, mean it, let her hear it in my voice. These are the small things. The daily practice. The spiral that continues, that must continue, that is the only immortality we have—the continuation, the next morning, the next apple, the next attempt to peel it without breaking, without crying, without needing anyone to finish what we started.

I will try again tomorrow. I will try to be worthy of the trying. I will carry the weight of all my previous selves, the child, the teenager, the young woman with her broken peel and her crumble and her cardigan, and I will move forward into whatever comes next, uncertain, hopeful, alive to the possibility that the next thing might be better, might be different, might be enough.

It is enough. It has to be. We keep going because we must, because the alternative is unthinkable, because the light is still here, still changing, still offering its temporary gold to anyone awake enough to receive it.

I am awake. I am here. I am writing.

That is all. That is everything.

samples.result:
The Weight of Unsent Messages

I have a folder on my phone. It's called "Drafts" but it's really a graveyard. Forty-seven messages I started and abandoned. Some are apologies I couldn't finish. Some are confessions I was too afraid to send. One is just the word "hey" typed seventeen times, each version deleted before I could commit to any of them.

We talk about the things we *do* say. The arguments, the declarations, the carefully worded texts at 2 AM. But nobody talks about the architecture of silence. The way a conversation can hang in the air, heavy as weather, while both people pretend to be fine.

My grandmother used to say that the tongue is a fire, and I think she meant it literally. Words burn going down. They burn coming out. The space between intention and utterance is where most of our lives actually happen—that vast, unmapped territory where we rehearse conversations that will never occur, where we forgive people in our heads who don't know they need forgiving, where we practice being brave and usually fail.

I think about this when I see people arguing in restaurants. The performative anger, the way they raise their voices to be heard by strangers. I wonder what they're really fighting about. Usually it's not the thing. It's the thing beneath the thing, the thing they can't name, the thing that would require them to be vulnerable in a way that feels like dying.

There's a particular loneliness to being understood too well. When someone finishes your sentences, when they know what you're going to say before you do. It's intimate, yes, but it's also a kind of erasure. The self needs friction to exist. Without resistance, without the gap between what I mean and what you hear, I become a ghost haunting my own life.

I used to write letters. Real letters, with stamps and envelopes and the delicious delay of days between sending and receiving. You had to mean what you wrote. You couldn't take it back, couldn't edit, couldn't pretend you said something kinder than you did. The imperfection was the point. The ink dried. The words were yours now, out in the world, doing whatever damage or healing they would do without your supervision.

Now everything is provisional. The little "typing..." indicator that appears and disappears like a heartbeat. The read receipts that turn blue and feel like accusations. The ability to delete, to unsend, to pretend the conversation never happened. We've built a world where commitment is optional, where every interaction is a draft, where we can curate our selves with the same anxiety we once reserved for job interviews.

I don't know if this is better or worse. I only know that I miss the weight of paper. The way a letter could arrive and change everything, or arrive and change nothing, but either way it *arrived*. It existed in the world as a physical fact. You couldn't unwrite it. You couldn't pretend you were never afraid, never hopeful, never alone in your room at night composing sentences to someone who might never read them.

There's a poem by Mary Oliver I keep returning to. "Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?" The question assumes we have plans. That we're architects of our own becoming. But most days I feel more like weather—happening to myself, surprised by my own moods, unable to control the pressure systems moving through me.

Maybe that's what the unsent messages are really about. Not fear, exactly. Recognition. The dawning awareness that we are all just drafts of ourselves, constantly revising, never quite finished, hoping someone will love the version we're currently working on.

I sent one of those forty-seven messages last week. The one that was just "hey." I added three more words. "I've been thinking about you." The response came in four minutes. We talked for an hour. Neither of us mentioned the years of silence, the messages started and abandoned, the careful choreography of almost-intimacy.

But I think we both knew. The subtext is always there, humming beneath the text. The weight of everything we don't say, pressing down on everything we do.

The folder is still there. Forty-six messages now. I'll probably never send them. Some things are better left as practice, as rehearsal, as the private language we develop with our own becoming. The self needs its shadows. The unsaid needs its space.

Tomorrow I'll write something new. Start and stop. Delete and begin again. This is the work. Not the sending, but the preparing. Not the arrival, but the journey toward it, however many times we turn back.

The tongue is a fire. But so is the silence that feeds it. Both can warm us. Both can burn. The trick, I'm learning, is knowing which one we need, moment to moment, word by word, in the one wild and precious life we have to figure out how to live.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The Weight of Unsent Messages

I have a folder on my phone called "Drafts I'll Never Send." It contains forty-seven messages. Some are apologies. Some are explanations. A few are just the word "hey" followed by nothing, the digital equivalent of clearing your throat in an empty room.

The oldest one is from 2019. It's to someone I loved who is now a stranger, and the message reads: *I keep thinking about the way you laughed at that terrible joke in the diner. I wish I'd laughed harder.*

I don't know what I wanted from that message. Validation? Forgiveness? The impossible reversal of time? What I know is that I typed it, deleted it, typed it again, and finally let it sit there like a stone in my pocket, heavy and useless.

---

My grandmother used to say that words were like birds. Once you let them fly, you couldn't call them back. She was a practical woman who believed in mending socks and keeping your word and not speaking ill of the dead. She never understood why I would write letters and then burn them. "What's the point," she'd ask. "If you're not going to send it, why bother?"

I never had an answer good enough for her. The point, I suppose, is the making. The shaping of thought into something that could, in theory, be understood by another person. The point is the rehearsal of intimacy without the risk of it.

---

There's a theory that we are all writing our lives as we live them, constantly revising, constantly editing. The version of yourself that you present at work is different from the one at Thanksgiving dinner, different again from the one alone in your car singing badly to the radio. Which one is real? The theory says all of them, and none of them, and that the self is a story we tell to keep from falling apart.

I think about this when I read old journals. The person in those pages is recognizably me—same anxieties, same hopes, same tendency to overthink—but also completely foreign. She believed things I no longer believe. She wanted things I no longer want. She was, in some ways, braver. In other ways, more afraid.

I used to think this meant I was growing. Now I'm not so sure. Maybe I'm just accumulating. Maybe the self is less a story and more a palimpsest, layers of old selves showing through the new, never fully erased.

---

I have a friend who sends voice messages at 3 AM. Not to me—she doesn't know I know—but to someone, or to no one, I can't tell. The messages are fragments. A laugh. A sigh. The sound of her breathing. Once, a whispered "I'm sorry" that might have been meant for anyone.

She is the most guarded person I know. She has walls so high and so well-maintained that I sometimes forget she has a interior life at all. And yet, at 3 AM, she speaks into the void as if someone is listening. As if the act of speaking itself is enough, the content irrelevant.

I think about this when I feel the urge to reach out and then don't. The 3 AM voice message is a kind of prayer, I think. Not to God, but to the possibility of being heard. To the universe, which is mostly indifferent but occasionally, inexplicably, kind.

---

The word "saudade" is Portuguese. It has no exact English translation. It means a deep emotional state of nostalgic longing for something or someone that one loves, combined with the knowledge that that thing or person is gone, perhaps forever. It is not quite sadness. It is not quite melancholy. It is the ache of absence made into a word.

I felt it once, driving through the desert in New Mexico, listening to a song I'd heard a thousand times before and never really heard. The lyrics were simple—*I miss you, I miss you, I miss you*—but the way they were sung, the way the voice cracked on the last syllable, made me pull over and cry for twenty minutes in a rest stop parking lot.

I didn't miss anyone in particular. Or maybe I missed everyone. The version of myself who could cry that easily. The people I'd loved and lost. The people I'd never known but imagined. The whole vast architecture of connection that makes a life feel like a life.

Saudade is the word for the weight of all those unsent messages, I think. The love we couldn't express. The apologies we couldn't make. The versions of ourselves we couldn't become. It is the gravity of the heart, pulling us toward what we cannot have.

---

I am trying to write more. Not for publication, not for praise, but because I have noticed that when I don't write, the days blur together. Monday becomes Tuesday becomes Wednesday, and I wake up one morning surprised to find that months have passed, that I have been sleepwalking through my own life.

Writing is a way of paying attention. It is a way of saying: *this happened, this mattered, I was here.* Even if no one ever reads it. Even if it's just the word "hey" followed by nothing, the digital equivalent of clearing your throat in an empty room.

The drafts folder on my phone is a kind of archive. Forty-seven messages to people who will never see them. Forty-seven versions of myself, reaching out, pulling back, reaching out again. The self as a series of almosts, of maybes, of what-ifs.

I don't know if I'll ever send them. I don't know if I should. But I know that I wrote them, and that writing them changed something. Made the weight a little lighter. Made the room a little less empty.

The birds are still in the cage. But I've opened the door. That has to count for something.

samples.result:
The Weight of Unsent Messages

I have a folder on my phone. It's called "Drafts" but it's really a graveyard. Forty-seven messages I started and abandoned. Some are apologies that felt too small for the thing they were apologizing for. Some are declarations that felt too large for the person receiving them. One is just the word "hey" typed seventeen times, each version deleted, each version somehow worse than the last.

My grandmother used to say that some things are better left unsaid, and I used to believe her. Now I think she was wrong, or at least incomplete. Some things are better left *said badly* than left unsaid entirely. The silence becomes its own message. It calcifies. It becomes the thing you both pretend isn't there while it grows teeth.

I think about this when I'm lying in bed at 2 AM, thumb hovering over the send button, composing a message to someone I haven't spoken to in three years. The message would be honest. It would explain why I disappeared. It would take responsibility for the specific ways I failed them. It would ask for nothing, demand nothing, offer only the truth of what happened and why I was afraid.

I don't send it. I never send it. Instead I delete it, and then I type it again the next night, and the cycle continues until the words lose their meaning, until "I'm sorry" becomes just shapes on a screen, until I can't remember what I was sorry for.

There's a particular loneliness to this. Not the loneliness of being alone, which is honest and clean. The loneliness of being *almost* connected. Of having the door open, the light on, the phone in your hand, and still choosing the dark.

I wonder sometimes if the people I've lost would even want to hear from me. Maybe the silence is kinder. Maybe my apology would just reopen a wound they've finally learned to live with. Maybe I'm not trying to make amends. Maybe I'm just trying to make myself feel better, and the difference matters.

But then I remember the letter I found last year, written by my grandfather to my grandmother in 1962, the year before they married. He was in Korea. She was in Ohio. The letter was four pages long and he apologized for something small—a missed phone call, a harsh word—and he wrote about the way the light looked through the tent flap at dawn, and he wrote "I am thinking of you constantly" seventeen times, and I realized that love is mostly this. Love is the willingness to be ridiculous. To say the thing that makes you vulnerable. To send the message even when you're afraid of the answer.

He kept the letter. She kept it too, in a box with his medals and a lock of her hair from when she was nineteen. They were married for fifty-one years. I don't know if the letter saved anything, or started anything, or was just one small brick in a wall they built together. But I know they chose to keep it. They chose to remember that someone had once thought of them constantly, had once written it down, had once been brave enough to send it.

I'm trying to be braver. I'm trying to send the messages. Most of them still go unsent, but some get through. A text to my sister at midnight: "I love you, I'm proud of you, I'm sorry I'm not better at showing up." A voice memo to an old friend: "I miss you. I don't know how to fix it. I just wanted you to know." These are small things. They don't fix anything. But they're real, and they're mine, and they're out in the world now instead of trapped in the graveyard of my drafts.

The folder is smaller now. Forty-seven became forty-three became thirty-nine. Some messages I finally sent. Some I deleted for good, recognizing that the urge to speak was really just an urge to be heard, and that being heard by the wrong person, or in the wrong way, or at the wrong time, can be worse than silence.

I still have the "hey" that I typed seventeen times. I keep it as a reminder. Not of failure, but of the effort. Of the fact that I was trying, even when I didn't know how. Even when the words kept coming out wrong.

There's a Buddhist concept I read about once: the idea that we are all Buddhas, but we don't know it. We walk around with our enlightenment hidden, our wisdom buried, our capacity for compassion locked behind fear and habit and the stories we tell ourselves about who we are and what we deserve.

I think about this when I'm afraid to send the message. When I tell myself that I'm not worth the response, or that the other person is better off without me, or that love is a finite resource and I've already spent my share. These are stories. They're not true. They're just familiar, and familiarity feels like safety, even when it's really just a cage with the door left open.

The door is open. The light is on. The phone is in my hand.

I'm going to send something tonight. Something small. Something true. Something that might not matter to anyone but me, but that I need to put into the world before I forget how.

The weight of unsent messages is the weight of a life half-lived. I'm tired of carrying it. I'm tired of being afraid.

Hey. I'm still here. I'm sorry I disappeared. I'm trying to do better. I hope you are too.

samples.result:
The Weight of Unsent Letters

I keep a drawer for letters I never sent. Not the romantic kind, though there are a few of those too, yellowed now, the ink bleeding into something almost illegible. Mostly they're the ordinary cruelties and kindnesses we exchange without thinking—the sharp word at dinner, the compliment withheld, the apology that died in my throat when I realized it would change nothing.

My grandmother had a similar drawer, I discovered after she died. Hers was in the cedar chest at the foot of her bed, and hers were all sent. Dozens of them, tied with ribbon, addressed in her careful script to people long dead. She wrote to her husband every week for forty years after he passed. She wrote to her sister in Toledo. She wrote to me, letters I found too late, tucked inside books I was meant to inherit. *I am proud of you*, she wrote in 1987, when I was twelve and failing math and convinced the world was ending. *The world does not end. It continues, and so do you.*

I don't know why she never mailed them. Maybe she knew some things are too heavy for the postal service. Maybe she was practicing, in her way, the art of letting go without the finality of delivery. Or maybe she simply forgot, the way we forget so many important things, and found them years later when the forgetting had become its own kind of grace.

---

There's a particular silence that happens in houses where someone has recently died. Not the absence of sound, but a quality to the sound that remains—the refrigerator humming slightly too loud, the neighbor's dog barking at something invisible, your own breathing suddenly audible in the space where theirs used to be. I've been in that silence three times now. Each time, I've learned something I didn't want to know about how memory works, how it doesn't fade so much as reorganize itself, finding new pathways around the missing piece.

After my father died, I kept hearing his voice in the grocery store, in the particular way the automatic doors sighed open at Safeway. I would turn, expecting to see him examining avocados with the intensity he reserved for important decisions. The avocados were never important. He just liked to hold them, to feel their weight, to imagine their ripeness. *This one*, he would say, though he never bought the one he chose. *This one is ready.*

I bought it anyway, that first time. Ate it with salt, standing at the kitchen sink, crying in a way that felt borrowed from someone else. The avocado was perfect. The crying was not.

---

I have been thinking about forgiveness lately, or the performance of it. The way we say *I forgive you* when what we mean is *I am tired of being angry*, or *I want things to return to normal*, or *I have calculated that this resentment costs me more than it costs you*. The forgiveness that isn't forgiveness at all, but strategy, or exhaustion, or the slow erosion of caring.

My mother forgave my father for things I don't know the names of. I know only that she forgave him, that she spoke the word often, that she wore it like a talisman against the particular loneliness of their marriage. When he died, she said *I forgive him* at the funeral, to no one in particular, to the empty chair where he would have sat, to the priest who didn't ask. She said it again at the cemetery, to the dirt, to the sky, to whatever she believed was listening.

I wanted to ask her what she meant. I wanted to know if forgiveness was a door you walked through or a door you built to keep something out. I didn't ask. I was twenty-six and still learning that some questions, once asked, cannot be unasked, that the asking itself changes the answer you receive.

She died four years later. I found her letters then, too, though hers were different from my grandmother's. Hers were to me. Dozens of them, unsent, hidden in the back of her closet where the winter clothes lived. *I am afraid*, she wrote in one, dated 2003. *I am afraid of the silence you will leave when you go to college. I am afraid of being alone with your father. I am afraid that I have already lost you, that you are only visiting, that the real you is somewhere I cannot reach.*

I was visiting. I was always visiting, in my own life, in my own skin, in the particular performance of being someone's daughter that I had never quite mastered. I read the letters and felt the particular grief of being loved by someone who didn't know how to say it, who said it instead in the language of worry, of fear, of the things left unsaid because saying them felt too much like confession.

---

There is a tree outside my window. I don't know what kind. It loses its leaves in October and grows them back in April, and in between it stands naked against the sky, doing nothing, being nothing but itself. I have watched it for seven years now. I have named it, though I won't tell you the name, because some things are private even in confession. I have talked to it, on bad days, when talking to humans felt like too much work, too much risk of being misunderstood or of misunderstanding in return.

The tree does not answer. This is its gift. It does not offer advice or ask for explanations or pretend to understand what I cannot articulate. It simply stands, rooted in its particular patch of earth, drinking whatever rain comes, surviving whatever winter. I find this more comforting than I expected to. I find it more comforting than most of what humans offer, which is usually the performance of comfort, the *there, there*, the *it will be okay*, the words that mean *I am uncomfortable with your discomfort and need you to stop.*

The tree is comfortable with my discomfort. It has its own, I imagine—the insects that eat its leaves, the drought years, the lightning strike that scarred its trunk in 2019. It does not speak of these things. It simply continues, which is its own kind of eloquence, its own stubborn refusal to be anything other than what it is.

---

I am learning to be more tree-like. This is the project of my middle age, if I can call it that, if forty-two qualifies. I am learning to want less, to need less, to find my nourishment in smaller and more particular things. The particular way light hits the kitchen table at 7 AM. The particular sound of my neighbor's cat, yowling at 3 AM for reasons I will never know. The particular weight of a book in my hands, the particular smell of old paper, the particular silence that follows when I finish a chapter and have to decide whether to continue.

I am learning to let things go. The grudges, mostly. The imagined slights, the conversations I rehearse in the shower, the elaborate scenarios where I finally say the right thing and am finally understood. I am learning that understanding is not the point, that being understood is a kind of luxury I cannot afford, that the work of living is mostly the work of continuing without it.

My grandmother's letters taught me this, in their way. She wrote to the dead and did not send. She spoke to the absent and did not wait for reply. She found, I think, a kind of peace in the unilateral, in the love that asks nothing, that expects nothing, that simply persists in its own particular form, rooted and stubborn and utterly itself.

---

I will fill the remaining words with something useful, or something beautiful, or something that pretends to be either. The truth is I don't know what comes next. The truth is I am still learning how to write without knowing where I'm going, how to trust the process, how to believe that the words will find their shape if I simply keep my hand moving, keep my attention open, keep showing up for the work even when the work feels like nothing, like waste, like the particular silence of a house where someone has recently died.

But here is what I know. Here is what I have learned from the tree, from my grandmother, from the drawer of unsent letters and the cedar chest and the closet where my mother hid her fears. Here is what I want to say, finally, to all of them, to myself, to whatever reads this:

*I am here. I am still here. I am learning to be here without needing to be anywhere else, without needing to be anyone other than this particular collection of cells and memories and unsent words, this particular way of seeing the world, flawed and limited and utterly my own.*

*The world does not end. It continues, and so do I.*

*I forgive you. I forgive myself. I forgive the silence, the waiting, the words that never found their destination. They were sent, in the end. They were sent to the only place that could receive them: the air, the dark, the great indifferent tree that drinks whatever comes and asks for nothing in return.*

*I am the tree now. I am the letter unsent. I am the particular silence of a house where someone has recently died, and someone else has learned, finally, to live inside it.*

*This is enough. This has always been enough. This will be enough, until it isn't, and then I will learn something new, and begin again, and write the next thousand words, and the next, and the next, for as long as the writing writes me, for as long as I am here to be written.*

---

The Weight of Unsent Messages

I have a folder on my phone called "Drafts" that terrifies me. Not because of what's in it—though there is that—but because of what it represents. The gap between intention and action. The space where words go to almost become real.

There's one to my grandmother, started three years ago after she called me by my mother's name. I never finished it. She died in March. I still open it sometimes, thumb hovering over the delete key, unable to decide if erasing it would be a mercy or a second death.

There's one to a man I loved in another city, written in a hotel room at 2 AM, full of things I was too afraid to say while his breathing was warm against my neck. We don't speak anymore. The draft ends with "I think about you when—" and then nothing. The ellipsis feels honest. Some thoughts don't need completion to be true.

There's one to myself, from when I was twenty-three and believed that if I just worked hard enough, I could outrun the person I was becoming. I was wrong about that. But I was right about something else: I was becoming someone. Just not who I planned.

---

My neighbor's dog barks at 6 AM every morning. I used to hate it. Now I wake up before it, lying in the dark, waiting for the sound that means the world is still turning, still ordinary, still mine to inhabit. The dog's name is Biscuit. I've never met Biscuit. I know this about him because my neighbor talks to him through the window. "Morning, Biscuit. Big day ahead?" And Biscuit, who is apparently a very good listener, does not bark in response. Just wags, I imagine, the way dogs do.

I think about Biscuit when I can't sleep. Not because he's remarkable, but because he's witnessed. Someone sees him every morning. Someone speaks to him. Someone expects him to be there, to be himself, to continue.

---

I found a receipt in my coat pocket from a pharmacy, dated fourteen months ago. I don't remember buying anything. The total was $4.87. I must have bought gum, or batteries, or something I needed and immediately forgot. The banality of it moves me. Someone was me, walking through a store, making a decision, living a life that has already passed into the past tense. I was there. I was *there*. And now I can only prove it with a slip of thermal paper, fading in my palm.

---

My mother calls every Sunday. We talk about the weather, about her garden, about whether I'm eating enough. She asks if I'm seeing anyone. I say "working on it," which is a lie, which she knows is a lie, which we both pretend is not a lie because the alternative is a conversation we're not ready to have. She was thirty when she married my father. I am thirty-four. The math embarrasses me. As if time were a test I'm failing by not having replicated her timeline exactly.

But here is what I don't say: that I am happy. That the life I'm building, slow and strange and mostly solitary, is the first one that has ever felt like mine. That I wake up without dread most days. That I have learned to be alone without being lonely, which is a skill she never needed to learn, which makes her love for me complicated in ways I'm only beginning to understand.

---

There's a woman at the coffee shop who reads the same book every Tuesday. I've watched her progress through it over eight months. She's on page 340 now. She always orders the same thing: oat milk latte, extra hot, no foam. She sits in the corner by the window and underlines passages with a pencil. I have never seen her speak to anyone. I have never spoken to her. We are two people sharing a space, performing solitude in parallel, and I find it more intimate than most of my actual relationships.

Last week, she left her pencil on the table. I almost said something. Instead, I watched her walk to the counter, realize her mistake, turn back, retrieve it. The small drama of her forgetting, her noticing, her correcting. I wanted to be the person who handed it to her. I wanted to be the reason she smiled at a stranger. I did nothing. She did not smile. But I carry the moment with me, the version of myself who almost spoke, the version of her who almost received.

---

I am afraid of becoming my father. Not the man he was—kind, tired, disappointed in ways he never showed—but the *idea* of him, the weight of expectation that sits on my shoulders like a hand I can't see. He wanted me to be practical. To be safe. To be *fine*. I am none of those things, or I am all of them, depending on the day, depending on who's asking, depending on whether I've had coffee yet.

He died believing I would figure it out. I think about that often. The faith of it. The absolute certainty that I would, eventually, become someone he would recognize. I am still becoming. I am still unrecognizable to myself, some mornings, staring into the mirror and wondering who is looking back. But I am trying. The trying is the only inheritance I know how to accept.

---

The 1000 words are almost up. I have written about drafts and dogs and receipts and mothers and strangers in coffee shops. I have written about fear and time and the small mercies of ordinary mornings. I have not written about the thing I thought I would write about when I started, which was the dream I had last night, which I have already forgotten except for the feeling it left: the sense of having been somewhere important, with someone important, and waking up to find that importance had evaporated like breath on glass.

But that's the nature of dreams. They are real only while they last. And then they become stories we tell ourselves, or don't, depending on whether we need them.

I need this one. I needed to write it. I needed to fill the space, to make something from the noise, to prove that I was here, that I am here, that the words can still come if I let them, if I stop trying to control them, if I just let them be what they want to be.

Goodnight, drafts. Goodnight, Biscuit. Goodnight, mother, wherever you are, whatever you're growing in your garden. Goodnight, stranger with the pencil. Goodnight, self, whoever you are becoming.

I am still here. I am still trying. That is enough for now. That has to be enough.

samples.result:
The Weight of Unsent Messages

I keep a folder on my phone called "Drafts I'll Never Send." It's not romantic, not really. Just a graveyard of almosts. The apology I wrote to my father three years ago, back when I still thought time was something we had plenty of. The explanation to my college roommate about why I stopped answering her calls. The love letter to someone who moved to Portland and never looked back. Each one sits there, timestamped, waiting for a courage I haven't found.

My therapist says I should delete them. "They're keeping you in the past," she said last Tuesday, her voice gentle in that way therapists have, like she's afraid of startling a bird. But I can't. What if I need them? What if, someday, I want to remember exactly how I felt? The specific ache of wanting to be understood and not knowing how to ask.

---

There's a woman who lives in my building who waters her plants every morning at 6:15. I know this because I'm usually awake then, staring at the ceiling, listening to the radiator clank like it's trying to communicate in some ancient language. She has a balcony garden—tomatoes, basil, something purple I can't identify from three floors down. Last week she looked up. I was standing at my window in my underwear, coffee going cold in my hand. She waved. I waved back. We've never spoken. I don't know her name. But I think about her when I'm sad, this stranger with her ritual of care, her tomatoes growing toward the sun.

I wonder if she knows I watch her. If she's ever wondered about the person in 4B who appears at the window at the same time, who seems to be waiting for something.

---

My grandmother used to say that everyone carries a stone in their pocket. "It's the weight of what you haven't said," she told me once, when I was twelve and crying because a boy had called me ugly in front of the whole cafeteria. She made me tea with too much sugar and told me about her own stone. She'd never told my grandfather she loved him. Not once, in forty-three years of marriage. She thought he knew. She thought it was obvious. He died on a Tuesday. She found a letter in his desk drawer, dated 1987, where he'd written that he'd loved her from the moment he saw her crying in the rain outside the library. He'd never sent it either.

"Stones are heavy," she said. "But they're also proof you felt something."

She died last spring. I found her stone in her jewelry box, wrapped in a handkerchief. It was just a smooth river rock, gray and unremarkable. I keep it on my desk now. Sometimes I hold it when I'm writing something difficult. Sometimes I forget it's there.

---

I went to the ocean last month. Not a vacation—just a Tuesday, a train ticket, three hours of my life I decided to spend differently. The water was gray and cold and absolutely indifferent to me. I walked along the shore and found a message in a bottle. Not a romantic message, not a plea for rescue. Just a grocery list: eggs, milk, bread, the cat's medication. Someone had written it on the back of a receipt from a store I'd never heard of, in a town I couldn't place. The bottle was sealed with wax. I opened it. I read it. I put it back in the water and watched it bob away.

I don't know why I'm telling you this. Maybe because it felt like a secret. Maybe because I wanted to be the kind of person who finds messages in bottles, even boring ones. Maybe because I'm lonely in a way I don't know how to fix.

---

There's a theory that we're all writing the same story, over and over, in different languages. The hero's journey. The fall and redemption. The moment of recognition. I used to believe it, that there was some shape to a life, some architecture. Now I think we're just making it up as we go, and the stories we tell afterward are attempts to impose order on chaos. The drafts I never send. The stones we carry. The woman with her tomatoes. The grocery list in a bottle. None of it means anything. All of it means everything.

I'm going to delete the folder. Not today. Maybe tomorrow. Or next week. When I'm ready to stop being the person who needed those words, who needed to have wanted them so badly.

The ocean took my grocery list. Maybe it will take my drafts too, if I let it. Maybe that's what water is for—carrying away what we can't say, what we can't keep, what we can't bear to throw away ourselves.

I'll stand at the window tomorrow morning. 6:15. I'll wave at the woman with the tomatoes. Maybe she'll wave back. Maybe, someday, we'll speak. Maybe I'll find another stone, or lose the one I have, or learn to carry it more lightly.

The radiator will clank. The coffee will go cold. The day will begin, indifferent and ordinary and absolutely mine.

That's enough. That's always been enough.

The Weight of Unsent Messages

I keep a folder on my phone called "Drafts I'll Never Send." It's not romantic, not really. Just a graveyard of half-finished thoughts, apologies that curdled into silence, jokes that died on the vine. There's one to my mother from three years ago. "Mom, I know you're worried about—" and then nothing. I don't remember what I was going to say. Probably something about my job, or my apartment, or the way I've started drinking wine alone on Tuesdays and calling it self-care.

The folder has 47 items. I counted once, then stopped counting. Some are to people I haven't spoken to in years. Some are to people I see every day. The proximity doesn't matter. What matters is the gap between what I feel and what I say, and how that gap widens with each passing hour until the words feel foreign, like speaking a language I once knew but have forgotten.

My therapist says I have trouble with vulnerability. She says it like it's a diagnosis, which I suppose it is. "You intellectualize your emotions," she told me last month. "You turn them into essays instead of letting them be messy." I nodded. I always nod. Then I went home and wrote a 2,000-word analysis of why I nod in therapy sessions.

There's something about the written word that feels safer. It can be edited. It can be deleted. It can sit in a folder, unseen, until the phone dies and takes it with it. Speaking is different. Speaking is immediate. Speaking is a commitment. You can't unsay the thing you blurted out at 2 AM when the wine has loosened your tongue and your defenses.

I think about my father sometimes. He died when I was twenty-three, which is young enough to still feel like a child and old enough to know better. We didn't speak for the last two years of his life. There was a fight. There are always fights. I don't remember what it was about anymore, only the shape of it—his voice rising, mine shutting down, the door closing with a sound like finality. I wrote him a letter after he died. I never sent it. It's in the folder. I read it sometimes, and I can't tell if it's forgiveness or just more performance, another essay dressed up as grief.

The thing about unsent messages is that they become their own kind of relationship. You maintain a version of someone in your head, a dialogue that only exists in one direction. My mother, in my drafts, is always understanding, always patient. The real her is more complicated. She calls too often and not often enough. She asks about my love life with a hopefulness that makes me want to hide. She sends me articles about depression and anxiety, as if I haven't spent my adult life managing both. I love her. I don't know how to tell her that without it sounding like a complaint.

I met someone last winter. Her name was Clara, and she had a laugh that sounded like breaking glass—sharp and surprising and a little dangerous. We talked for six hours in a bar that was closing around us, and I felt something unlock in my chest, some door I'd forgotten was there. Then I went home and wrote her a message that was too long, too earnest, too *much*. I deleted it. I wrote another. Deleted that too. By morning, I'd convinced myself that I'd imagined the connection, that it was just the whiskey and the loneliness and the particular sadness of a Tuesday in January.

She texted me three days later. "Had fun last night. We should do it again." I stared at the message for an hour. Then I wrote: "Yeah. Definitely." Three words. Safe. Forgettable. She didn't reply. I told myself that was fine. I told myself a lot of things.

The folder grows. It's almost full now, 47 drafts taking up space I'll never reclaim. Sometimes I wonder what would happen if I sent them all at once, a burst of honesty that would probably destroy every relationship I have. Or maybe it would save them. Maybe the weight of all that unsaid is what's actually killing us, slowly, one unspoken truth at a time.

I don't know. I'm still writing. That's the thing about words—they keep coming, even when no one's listening. Especially then.

The Weight of Unsent Letters

I have a drawer. Everyone has one, I think—that place where words go to rest. Mine is the bottom left of my desk, the one that sticks in summer when the humidity swells the wood. Inside: birthday cards I never mailed, apology letters I wrote at 3 AM and abandoned by morning, a love letter to someone who moved to Portland and a thank-you note to my grandmother that I meant to send before she died.

I keep them anyway. Not because I'm sentimental, exactly. Because throwing them away feels like admitting the words never mattered, and I'm not ready for that admission.

---

My neighbor's dog barks at 6 AM every day. I've started to think of it as a kind of alarm clock, though I don't wake up grateful. The dog is small, yappy, the kind that trembles when thunder comes. I've never seen it without its owner, a woman who wears the same gray coat regardless of season. They walk past my window at 6:15, her brisk, him straining at the leash, nose to the ground, reading the news of the night—pee mail, I suppose, the ancient language of dogs.

Sometimes I wonder what they talk about on these walks. Whether she tells him about her day, her worries, the way she sometimes cries in the shower. Whether he understands. Whether anyone understands.

---

I ate cereal for dinner last night. Not because I was sad, exactly. Because the milk was about to expire and I hate waste, and because there's something honest about eating something that requires no performance. No chopping, no timing, no pretending I'm the kind of person who plans meals. Just pour, eat, rinse.

My mother used to say that cooking was love made visible. I think she meant it. I think she believed it. But I've watched people cook elaborate meals for people they resented, and I've eaten sad sandwiches made by hands that loved me completely. The correlation isn't as strong as we'd like.

---

There's a tree outside my window that I've started to notice. Not because it's remarkable—it's a maple, ordinary, losing its leaves in that slow way trees do—but because I've been here long enough to watch it change. Last spring it budded late, worried me. This summer it held its green longer than the others on the street. Now it's burning, that particular orange that looks almost lit from within.

I don't know its name. I don't know if it has one. But I've started to think of it as mine, this small claim on something that will outlast me, that was here before me, that will keep its slow calendar long after I've stopped keeping mine.

---

I met someone recently who asked what I do. I said I write, which is true but incomplete, the way saying I breathe is true but doesn't explain why I keep doing it. They nodded like they understood. Maybe they did. Maybe they also writes, or paints, or builds things, or parents children with the same desperate hope that the work will matter.

We talked for two hours. I don't remember most of it. I remember that they laughed with their whole body, that they had a scar on their chin from a bicycle accident at age seven, that they were afraid of the ocean but loved to swim in it anyway. I remember thinking: this is what I forget to do, this paying attention, this letting someone be strange and specific in front of me without rushing to categorize them.

I meant to ask for their number. I didn't. I'm still deciding whether that was wisdom or cowardice.

---

The word "almost" is a small violence. Almost loved. Almost left. Almost said the thing that would have changed everything. I think about it often, the almosts, the way they accumulate like dust, invisible until you try to breathe.

My father almost came to my graduation. Almost called on my birthday. Almost, almost, almost—until the word loses its meaning, becomes just a sound, a placeholder for the life he didn't live with me.

I don't forgive him. I don't know if I need to. But I've stopped waiting for the almost to become real. That's something, I think. That's the small work of continuing.

---

I want to tell you about the light in my apartment at 4 PM in October. How it comes in low and gold, turns everything it touches into something precious, temporary, already leaving. I want to tell you because I think you might understand, or because I need to believe someone would.

The light hits the dust on my windowsill. It makes the dust beautiful. This is the trick of it, the way attention transforms. Not the thing itself, but the noticing. The willingness to see what's already there.

I think about this when I feel invisible. When I feel like no one is looking, no one would miss me, no one would notice if I stopped. The light doesn't care if I'm watching. It comes anyway. It makes the dust beautiful anyway.

Maybe that's enough. Maybe that's everything.

---

I'm afraid of becoming someone who doesn't try. Not failure—failure is fine, failure is information. But the slow settling into a life that's smaller than the one I imagined, the gradual acceptance that the big things won't happen, the dreams will shrink to fit the available space.

I'm afraid of my own patience. How good I've become at waiting, at making do, at telling myself that contentment is enough.

But I'm also afraid of the opposite: the person who burns everything down chasing something better, who can't stay, who mistakes restlessness for vitality. I've known people like that. I've been that person, briefly, in my twenties, when leaving felt like the only honest choice.

I don't know how to be in the middle. How to want things without desperation, how to rest without surrender. I'm learning, I think. Or I'm telling myself that. The difference matters less than I used to believe.

---

Tonight I'll probably watch something I've seen before. A show, a movie, something that requires no decision, no risk, no possibility of surprise. I'll eat something easy. I'll go to bed too late and wake up tired. I'll do it again tomorrow.

This is not a tragedy. This is not a triumph. This is the shape of a life, the ordinary miracle of continuing, of finding small reasons to stay, of letting the light in when it comes, of noticing the tree, of keeping the unsent letters in their drawer, just in case, just because.

The dog will bark at 6 AM. The woman in the gray coat will walk past my window. The maple will burn a little brighter, then let go, then wait for spring.

I will be here. I will notice. I will try, again, to say the true thing, to send the letter, to ask for the number, to risk the almost becoming real.

That's the work, I think. Not the big gesture. The small, repeated choice to pay attention, to hope, to continue.

---

samples.result:
The Weight of Unsent Messages

I have a folder on my phone. It's called "Drafts" but it's really a graveyard. Forty-seven messages I started and abandoned. Some are apologies that felt too small for the wound. Some are declarations that felt too large for the room. One is just the word "hey" typed seventeen times, each instance deleted, each deletion a small death.

We don't talk about this, do we? The architecture of almost-communication. The way we build elaborate structures in our minds—conversations we rehearse in the shower, letters we compose at 3 AM, the perfect response we craft while the other person is still talking—and then we let them dissolve. Evaporate. Become nothing.

My grandmother kept a shoebox of unsent letters. I found it after she died, tied with a ribbon she'd saved from some anniversary, some gift. Inside were letters to her sister, who'd died in 1987. Letters to her husband, who'd died in 2003. Letters to me, written when I was twelve and angry about something I don't remember, something that felt like the end of the world. She never sent any of them. She told me once, when I was maybe twenty, that some things are better kept inside. "The saying makes it real," she said. "And real things have weight."

I didn't understand then. I thought she was being poetic, or sad, or both. Now I think she was describing a kind of mercy. The mercy of not making things permanent. Of letting them exist in the liminal space between thought and action, where they can't hurt anyone, where they can't be misunderstood, where they remain exactly what you intended rather than what the other person received.

But there's another mercy, isn't there? The mercy of sending. Of letting the weight exist in the world, of trusting that it can be held by someone else. I think about this when I read old text messages, the ones I actually sent. The clumsy ones. The ones sent at wrong moments, to wrong people, saying things I meant but didn't mean to mean in that way. They're embarrassing. They're human. They're proof that I was here, trying, failing, trying again.

The philosopher Emmanuel Levinas wrote about the face of the Other—the way another person's face calls you to responsibility, demands that you respond. I think about this when I'm tempted to delete. The face isn't there, not really. It's a screen, a cursor blinking. But the possibility of the face is there. The possibility that someone is waiting, that they need to hear this, that the weight of the unsent thing is crushing them too.

I sent one of those drafts last week. It was to someone I hurt, years ago, in a way I've never properly acknowledged. The draft had been sitting there for two years. I rewrote it eleven times. I almost deleted it again. But I sent it. And the response—not forgiveness, not yet, maybe never—was something else. It was acknowledgment. It was the beginning of a conversation that might, eventually, become a relationship again. Or might not. But it was real. It had weight. It existed outside my head.

My grandmother's letters are still in the shoebox. I keep it in my closet. Sometimes I read them. They're beautiful, in their way—full of love and regret and the particular loneliness of a woman who believed that some things should remain private. But I wonder, sometimes, what would have happened if she'd sent them. If her sister had known, before she died, that she was missed. If her husband had known, in his final years, that he was still loved. If I had known, at twelve, that she understood my anger, that she wasn't afraid of it, that she loved me through it.

The weight of unsent messages is a particular kind of grief. It's the grief of possible selves, possible relationships, possible versions of the world that never came to be. We carry it without naming it. We call it shyness, or pride, or wisdom. Sometimes it is those things. But sometimes it's just fear. The fear that the weight will be too much. The fear that we'll be misunderstood. The fear that the other person won't be able to hold what we're offering.

I'm trying to be braver. To send the messages. To let them have weight. To trust that the world can hold more than I think it can. It's not easy. The drafts folder is still full. But it's smaller now. Forty-three messages instead of forty-seven. Progress, of a sort. The kind that doesn't show up in any metric, that no one else can see. The kind that matters anyway.

There's a poem by Mary Oliver that I return to, about a man who finds a snake in his path and, instead of killing it, lets it pass. "I had no right, I knew, to leave it there," he says. "To let it escape into the world." I think about this when I delete. When I let something escape into the world of almost, of not-quite, of never-was. The snake is still there, in the grass. It's still real. But it's not in the world I have to be responsible for.

I want to be responsible. I want to let things escape into the world and stay there. To be changed by them. To change others. This is the work, I think. Not the perfection of the message, but the sending. Not the guarantee of understanding, but the risk of it. Not the weightlessness of the draft, but the gravity of the sent.

My grandmother is gone now. Her letters remain. I read them and I feel her presence, her particular way of loving—careful, contained, real in its own bounded way. But I also feel the absence of what might have been. The conversations that never happened. The weight that never got shared.

I don't want to end up like that. I don't want my closet to be full of shoeboxes. I want to send. I want to be misunderstood. I want to hold other people's weight, and let them hold mine. It's terrifying. It's necessary. It's the only way I know to be fully here, in this world, with these people, in this time that we have and won't have again.

The cursor blinks. The draft waits. I will write something. I will send it. I will let it be real.
