The letters don't change. They accumulate like sediment, layer upon layer of things I needed to say but couldn't, in the moment, face-to-face.

I think about this sometimes when I'm at parties, making small talk, laughing at jokes I don't find funny. There's a version of me that exists in these letters. She's more honest. She's also more alone. She says things like "I am afraid I am becoming someone I don't recognize" and "I don't know how to be loved" and "I think I need help but I don't know how to ask for it."

The me at parties says "I'm fine, thanks, just busy with work." Both are true. Both are incomplete. The question is which incompleteness I can live with.

---

My neighbor's dog barks at 3 AM. Not every night, but often enough that I've started to think of it as a kind of clock, a reminder that the world continues its indifferent rotation. I used to get angry. Now I find it almost comforting, this proof that something else is awake, something else is struggling with the dark.

I have trouble sleeping. It's not insomnia exactly—I sleep, eventually, deeply, the kind of sleep that leaves you drooling on your pillow—but the getting there is a negotiation. My mind wants to review the day, rehearse conversations, compose emails I'll never send. It wants to solve problems that don't exist yet. It wants to be anywhere but here, in this bed, in this body, in this particular moment that will never come again.

I've tried everything. White noise. Meditation apps with soothing voices. Reading until my eyes burn. Counting sheep, which I've always found absurd—why sheep? Why not, I don't know, tax forms? Something actually boring. Last week I tried counting backwards from 1000 in French, which I studied in high school and have mostly forgotten. *Mille, neuf cent quatre-vingt-dix-neuf, neuf cent quatre-vingt-dix-huit...* I made it to about 850 before my mind wandered to whether the French actually count down differently, whether there's some cultural reason for the awkwardness of *quatre-vingt-dix-neuf*, and then I was thinking about my high school French teacher, Mrs. Patterson, who wore too much perfume and once cried in class when she talked about her divorce, and then I was awake again, fully, staring at the ceiling.

---

There's a photograph of me at seven that I can't look at without feeling something I don't have a name for. I'm standing in front of a birthday cake, mouth open in that particular way children have, half-laugh, half-scream, the candle smoke still curling upward. My eyes are bright. I look, in that photograph, like someone who believes that good things will keep happening, that the world is fundamentally generous, that love is simple and available and enough.

I don't know when that changed. I don't know if it changed gradually, like erosion, or all at once, like a door closing. I know that I spent years trying to get back to that girl, as if she were a place I could return to, a version of myself I could resurrect through effort and intention. I don't think she's coming back. I think she was a kind of grace, temporary, given to children so they can survive the knowledge of what's coming.

But I keep the photograph. I keep it in the same drawer as the letters, though it's not a letter. It's a question, really. *Who were you? What did you know that I've forgotten?*

---

I went to the doctor last month for a physical. Everything was fine, the doctor said. Blood pressure good, cholesterol good, "you're in great shape for someone your age." I'm thirty-four. I don't know what that means, great shape for thirty-four. I wanted to ask if he meant I was doing well compared to other thirty-four-year-olds, or if he was surprised I wasn't falling apart, or if he was just being polite. I didn't ask. I said thank you and scheduled my next appointment and left.

In the parking lot I sat in my car for ten minutes. I wasn't crying. I wasn't anything, really. Just sitting. The doctor had been kind, efficient, forgettable. He would not remember me tomorrow. This is the arrangement we've made, this transaction of care: I pay, he examines, we both pretend it matters more than it does. I don't blame him. I don't blame me. But I felt, sitting there, the particular loneliness of being known by no one, of being a body that functions, a set of numbers on a chart, a brief entry in a database that will eventually be deleted.

I drove home. I made dinner. I watched a show I didn't really follow. I went to bed.

---

My mother calls on Sundays. We talk about the weather, about my sister's new job, about whether I've eaten enough vegetables. She asks if I'm dating anyone. I say no, not seriously, and she says well, you're still young, you have time, and I say yes, I know, I have time, and we both know that time is not the issue, that the issue is something else, something we don't have words for, something that lives in the pauses between her questions and my answers.

I love her. I don't know how to tell her. I don't know if she knows. I think about the letter in my drawer, the one that begins "I don't call enough because—" and I can't finish it. I can't finish it because I don't know what comes after the because. Because I'm afraid? Because I'm ashamed? Because I don't know how to be the person she wants me to be, the person I was supposed to become, the son who calls more, who visits more, who is more grateful, more present, more *there*?

She's getting older. I can see it, the way she moves, the way she forgets words sometimes, mid-sentence, and has to start over. I want to tell her things. I want to tell her that I think about her constantly, that I carry her with me, that she is the reason I am who I am, for better and worse. I want to tell her that I am afraid, that I am lonely, that I don't know how to live the life I have. I want to tell her that I love her, that I have always loved her, that the not-calling is not a measure of that love, that it's something else, something broken in me, something I'm trying to fix.

Instead I say "I'm fine, Mom, how are you?" and she says "I'm good, I'm good, just busy" and we talk about the weather some more.

---

There's a man I see at the coffee shop. I don't know his name. I've never spoken to him. He comes in around 7:30, orders a black coffee, sits in the corner with a book. He's maybe sixty, with a beard that's gone mostly gray, and glasses that he keeps pushing up his nose. He reads for an hour, maybe two, then leaves. I've started timing my own arrival to overlap with his, though I would never admit this, even to myself, quite so baldly.

I don't want to be his friend. I don't want to know his story. I want, I think, to see someone else being alone in a way that looks peaceful, that looks chosen. He doesn't look at his phone. He doesn't look around the room, waiting, hoping. He just reads, and drinks his coffee, and exists in a way that seems complete unto himself.

I've started bringing my own book, though I don't read it. I sit near him, close enough to see the titles, far enough to seem uninterested. *The Brothers Karamazov*. *Austerlitz*. *The Overstory*. Books I've read, mostly, or started, or bought and abandoned. I pretend to read. I watch him, out of the corner of my eye, and I try to learn something. I try to learn how to be alone without it being a failure, a waiting, a gap to be filled.

He never looks at me. This is probably for the best. If he did, if he smiled, if he said hello, I don't know what I would do. I think I would panic. I think I would leave and not come back, because the spell would be broken, because he would become a person instead of a lesson, and I don't know how to be a person around other people.

---

I went to my father's funeral last year. I don't talk about this much. There's a version of me that existed before, and a version that exists after, and they don't quite connect. The funeral was small. He'd outlived most of his friends, his siblings, his wife—my mother, divorced from him for twenty years, present but distant, performing grief in a way that felt borrowed, rehearsed. I gave a eulogy. I don't remember what I said. I remember the sound of my own voice, strange in the quiet church, and I remember thinking that he couldn't hear me, that he was beyond hearing, beyond everything, and that this was the point, the whole point, that we speak to the dead because we cannot speak to the living, because the living are too complicated, too present, too likely to answer back.

After, people came up to me. *I'm so sorry for your loss. He was a good man. You must be devastated.* I said thank you, I'm fine, I'm handling it. I wasn't devastated. I was relieved, in a way I'm ashamed to admit. Relieved that it was over, that I wouldn't have to decide whether to visit him in the nursing home, whether to call, whether to pretend to care about a man who had never pretended to care about me. Relieved that the question was answered, finally, definitively, by something outside my control.

I cried later, in the hotel room, alone. Not for him. For me. For the child I was, waiting by the phone, hoping he would call, hoping he would show up, hoping he would be different than he was. For the adult I became, still waiting, still hoping, still unable to stop.

---

I don't know what I'm doing with this. With any of it. I write these words and I don't know who they're for. Not you, exactly, though I'm aware you're reading. Not me, though I'll read them later, maybe, in the drawer with the letters. Maybe they're for the man in the coffee shop, though he'll never see them. Maybe they're for my mother, or my father, or the version of myself at seven, standing in front of that cake, believing in good things.

I think, sometimes, that we are all just writing letters we'll never send, speaking to people who can't hear us, in languages we're still learning. I think that this is what it means to be human: to be perpetually in the middle of a sentence, never quite reaching the period, the full stop, the silence that would mean we're done, we're finished, we've said everything we need to say.

I don't believe this, not really. I believe that some things get said, eventually, or close enough. I believe that love, real love, finds its way through, despite our failures, our silences, our thousand unsent letters. I believe this because I have to, because the alternative is a loneliness I can't survive.

But I also believe that we carry our unsent letters with us, that they weigh something, that they shape us in ways we don't always recognize. I believe that the drawer will keep filling, that I will keep writing, that the words will keep coming, even when I don't know what to do with them, even when they seem to go nowhere, to mean nothing.

Tonight I'll go to bed. I'll lie in the dark and listen to my neighbor's dog, or the traffic, or the silence that follows them both. I'll try to sleep. I'll probably fail, at first. I'll think about the man in the coffee shop, and my mother, and the photograph of the girl at the birthday party. I'll think about all the things I haven't said, all the letters I'll write and not send, all the love I'll carry without delivering.

And then, maybe, I'll sleep. And tomorrow I'll wake up, and make coffee, and go to work, and try to be present, try to be here, try to be the person I was in that photograph, the one who believed that good things would keep happening.

I don't know if I believe it. But I'll try. I'll keep trying. Isn't that, in the end, all any of us can do?

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The Weight of Unsent Messages

I keep a folder on my phone called "Drafts I'll Never Send." It's not romantic, not really. Just a graveyard of half-finished thoughts, apologies that curdled into something else, observations about the light in the kitchen at 4 PM that I wanted to share with someone who no longer answers. There are forty-seven of them now. I checked this morning, out of some compulsion I don't fully understand.

Number 12 is to my mother. I started it three years ago after she said something at Thanksgiving that I still think about. "You're so quiet," she said, not unkindly, just noting it the way you'd note the weather. I wrote: *I'm not quiet, I'm just not saying the things I used to say to you.* Then I stopped. I don't know what I was waiting for. Permission, maybe. Or the right words. Or for the feeling to pass so I could pretend I'd never needed to say it at all.

There's a theory that we are all writing letters to people who can't receive them. That grief is just love with nowhere to go. I used to think that was too neat, too literary. But then I started noticing how many people I know who talk to the dead. Not in the séance way. In the ordinary way. Setting an extra place at dinner. Texting a number that will never light up. I did it for six months after my grandmother died, sending her links to articles I thought she'd like, recipes for the soup she made when I was sick. The phone would show "delivered" and I'd feel, briefly, like she'd seen it. Like she was still somewhere, just busy.

My friend Mara says I overthink everything. She's not wrong. Last week I spent twenty minutes composing a text to a man I went on one date with, trying to explain why I didn't want to see him again without making it sound like he'd done something wrong, which he hadn't, he was perfectly nice, I just didn't feel anything, which is its own kind of failure. I never sent it. Instead I sent: *Thanks for last night, take care.* The punctuation felt like a small violence.

I wonder sometimes what would happen if I sent them all. The folder, unleashed. Would it be cathartic or catastrophic? Probably both. Probably I'd regret most of them within the hour. But there's a part of me that wants to be known in my contradictions, in my need to explain myself to people who've already moved on. The drafts are more honest than I am in person. They contain the things I rehearse in the shower, the arguments I have with people who aren't there, the tenderness I can't quite access when someone is actually looking at me.

My therapist asked me last month what I'm afraid of. I said: *Being misunderstood.* She said: *By who?* And I didn't have an answer. That's the thing about these unsent messages. They're addressed to everyone and no one. They're me trying to solve a problem that doesn't exist, which is to say, trying to be understood before I've even figured out what I think.

I read somewhere that the average person speaks 16,000 words a day. I don't know if that's true, but I know I don't come close. Some days I go hours without saying anything that matters. The words pile up inside me, heavy as stones. I carry them around. They make me tired.

There's a draft to my father. I started it the day after he died, which was also the day I learned he'd been dead for three days before anyone found him. I wrote: *I'm sorry I didn't call more.* Then I wrote: *I'm sorry I called at all, sometimes, when I was angry, when I wanted you to fix things you couldn't fix.* Then I stopped. What do you say to someone who can't hear you, except the things you should have said when they could? It's a kind of cruelty, this timing. The universe's sense of humor, if it has one.

I think about the people who found him. The neighbor who noticed the mail piling up. The police officer who had to explain, gently, that no, he hadn't been sleeping, not really. I think about how death is so often a discovery rather than an event. Someone else's business, happening in a room you're not allowed to enter. I wanted to be there. I wanted to be the one to find him, as if that would have changed anything, as if my presence could have held him in his body a little longer, as if love is a physical force that can override physics.

It isn't. I know that. I know it intellectually, the way you know that the earth is round even when you're standing on flat ground. But some part of me is still standing in that apartment, still waiting for him to wake up, still believing that if I just say the right thing, if I just find the right words, he'll open his eyes and be surprised to see me there, surprised that I came, that I cared, that I was capable of showing up in the way he always wanted and I never quite managed.

The drafts don't help with that. They just make it more precise. They give shape to the wanting.

I have a draft to my ex. We were together for four years. We broke up two years ago, amicably, the way people say, as if amicable is a kind of victory. I wrote: *I still think about the life we were going to have.* Then: *I don't know if that's grief or just habit.* Then: *I don't know the difference anymore.* I deleted it. Started again. Deleted it again. Some things are too big for a text box. Some things need a room, a face, a body that can be held or not held, depending on what the moment requires.

I keep the drafts because deleting them feels like deleting evidence. Evidence of what? That I loved someone? That I failed to love them well? That I am a person who thinks in complete sentences even when no one is listening? I don't know. But I keep them. They're my archive. My proof that I was here, paying attention, trying to be honest in a world that makes honesty so difficult.

Tonight I'm going to dinner with Mara. She'll talk about her job, her new boyfriend, the book she's reading. I'll listen. I'll ask questions. I'll be present in the way I'm capable of being present, which is to say, mostly. Mostly there, with a small part of me elsewhere, composing sentences I won't say, saving them for a folder that grows and grows, a library of almosts, of might-have-beens, of love that arrived too late or left too soon or never quite learned how to stay.

After dinner, I'll walk home. The city will be loud and lit and indifferent to my small griefs. I'll pass a couple arguing on a stoop, a man talking to himself, a woman crying into her phone. We're all carrying our unsent messages. We're all trying to say the thing that matters before the moment passes, before the person leaves, before the light changes and we're someone else, someone who didn't need to say it after all.

I'll get home. I'll open my phone. I'll look at the folder, at the forty-seven drafts, and I'll add a forty-eighth. Something small. Something true. *The light in the kitchen at 4 PM is gold today. I thought of you.* I won't send it. But I'll keep it. I'll keep all of them. The evidence. The almost. The love that didn't find its destination but still, somehow, traveled somewhere. Somewhere I can visit, when I need to remember that I was here, that I tried, that I was capable of wanting something enough to write it down, even if I never learned how to let it go.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The Weight of Unsent Messages

I keep a folder on my phone called "Drafts I'll Never Send." It's not romantic, not really. Just a graveyard of half-finished thoughts, apologies that curdled into silence, jokes that died before they reached the punchline. There's one from 2019 to my grandmother, started the day after she died. "I meant to call you this weekend." I never finished it. What would I have said? That I was sorry I didn't visit more? That I was scared of hospitals? That I loved her and didn't know how to prove it?

We think we have time. That's the lie we tell ourselves at twenty-five, at forty, at sixty-five. Time is a currency we spend on the wrong things—scrolling, worrying, rehearsing conversations that never happen. My grandmother used to say, "The phone works both ways, sweetheart." She was right. I just didn't know how to pick it up.

---

There's a man who lives in my building who waters his plants every morning at 6 AM. I've never spoken to him. I know his routine better than I know my own. He has a fern that's struggling, browning at the edges, and I want to tell him about indirect light, about how ferns hate drafts. But what if he knows? What if he's experimenting? What if he doesn't want to talk to the woman who watches him from her window like a creep?

We are so alone together. Apartment buildings, coffee shops, airplanes—we share space but not selves. I think about the man with the fern sometimes when I'm lonely. He's not a solution. He's just proof that other people exist, that mornings happen, that someone is tending to something even when no one is watching.

---

My mother called last Tuesday. I let it go to voicemail. I was in the middle of something—nothing important, a video about how to fold a fitted sheet, which I still can't do. She left a message about her neighbor's dog dying. I listened twice. I didn't call back. I don't know why. I think I'm afraid of what she'll ask, what I'll have to admit. That I'm not happy? That I don't know what I'm doing? That I miss her, which feels like weakness, like failure, like something I should have outgrown by now?

She's seventy-three. I'm forty-one. When did we become this—two adults performing a relationship through missed calls and holiday cards? I want to be better. I want to be the daughter who calls on Sundays, who remembers birthdays, who shows up. But wanting and doing are different countries, and I keep getting lost at the border.

---

I found a notebook from 2003. I was nineteen, convinced I would be a writer, certain that my observations mattered. I read three pages and had to stop. Not because it was bad—some of it was surprisingly good—but because I was so *certain*. The certainty of youth, the belief that I understood anything. I don't write like that anymore. I write like someone who knows she'll be wrong, who expects to be misunderstood, who has learned that the point isn't to be right but to keep looking.

There's a poem in that notebook about a boy with green eyes who didn't love me back. I remember him. I remember the specific shade of his indifference. What I don't remember is why it mattered so much, why I thought my whole life would be measured against that one afternoon in a parking lot. We build monuments to our pain and call them wisdom. Maybe that's not entirely wrong. Maybe the monument is the point—proof that we were here, that we felt, that we survived the certainty that this would break us.

---

I'm afraid of becoming invisible. Not death—that's abstract, distant. Invisibility. The moment when people stop seeing you, when you become furniture, background, a voice they answer without hearing. I watch it happen to older people, especially women. The way they're talked over, talked at, dismissed as "cute" or "confused" or simply not there. I catch myself doing it too—rushing past the elderly man at the grocery store, assuming he won't have anything to say. Then I remember: I will be him. I will be her. The invisibility is coming for all of us, and we're building it brick by brick, assumption by assumption.

What's the opposite of invisible? Present. Attentive. Seen. I'm trying to practice. Asking the cashier how her day is and meaning it. Noticing the way light hits the building across the street at 4 PM. Writing down small things: the smell of rain on hot pavement, the particular silence of snow, the way my cat's purr sounds like a motor that's almost out of gas.

---

There's a theory that we're all living in a simulation. I don't believe it, not really. But I like the idea that someone—something—is watching, recording, caring about what happens to us. It makes the small kindnesses matter more. The way I hold the door. The way I let someone merge in traffic. The way I try, sometimes, to really listen.

My therapist says I have trouble with "emotional permanence." That when people leave the room, I forget they exist, forget that they love me, forget that I matter to them. It's true. I can feel it happening right now, writing this, alone in my apartment at midnight. The fear that no one will read this, that it doesn't matter, that I'm shouting into a void that doesn't even echo back.

But here's what I'm learning: the void echoes. Not always. Not clearly. But sometimes, late at night, someone else is awake, feeling the same loneliness, and they find your words and think *me too*, and for a moment, the distance between us shrinks. That's enough. That has to be enough. We keep writing, keep reaching, keep hoping that someone on the other end is listening.

---

I don't know how to end this. That's the truth of it. I started with unsent messages and I'm ending with the same fear—that I'll never send this either, that it will sit in drafts, that I'll delete it, that I'll convince myself it's not worth the risk of being seen.

But I'm writing it anyway. I'm writing all of it. The fern man, my mother's voicemail, the green-eyed boy, the notebook from 2003, the fear of invisibility, the hope that someone might understand.

This is what I have. This is what I am. Take it or leave it. I'm sending it anyway.

The Weight of Unsent Messages

I have a folder on my phone called "Drafts" that terrifies me. Not because of what's in it—mostly half-finished grocery lists, a recipe for soup I never made, a birthday message I wrote to my mother three years ago and never sent because I wasn't sure if she'd want to hear from me. The folder is a graveyard of almosts. The almost-I-love-yous. The almost-I'm-sorries. The almost-I-understand-now.

We live in an age of infinite communication and I think we've forgotten how to finish things. We leave people on read. We ghost. We craft the perfect response and then delete it because it feels too vulnerable, too much, too *real*. The cursor blinks. The draft saves itself. We move on.

My grandmother kept a shoebox of letters. Actual letters, with stamps and postmarks and her sister's handwriting slanting across the page. She wrote back to everyone. She kept the envelopes, sometimes, with the return addresses carefully preserved. When she died, we found letters from 1952. From a man she almost married. From a friend who moved to Oregon and never came back. She had kept the whole conversation alive, the back-and-forth of lives intersecting and then drifting apart, documented in ink.

I don't know if she ever felt the weight of those letters. The responsibility of response. The way a letter demands something from you—that you sit down, that you think, that you commit your thoughts to paper and trust the postal service to carry them across distance and time.

I think about this when I'm tempted to send something cruel in the heat of an argument, or something loving in the middle of the night when I'm lonely and the impulse feels urgent. The draft folder catches me. It says: *wait. Look at this again in the morning. Is this true? Is this kind? Is this necessary?*

Sometimes I do send things. Sometimes I don't. The unsent messages accumulate like sediment, layers of person I was trying to be, or needed to be, or failed to be.

There's a particular loneliness in realizing that someone you love has a folder like mine. That they wrote you something and didn't send it. That the version of you they needed to reach never got reached. You can't know this, of course. You can only wonder, sometimes, why the conversation went quiet. Why the friendship cooled. Why love, which felt so certain, simply... evaporated.

I'm trying to be better at finishing. At sending the message, even when it's imperfect. Especially when it's imperfect. The grocery list can stay unfinished. The soup recipe can wait. But the person on the other end—the one waiting for a sign that you still think about them, that you still care, that you're still here—they deserve the almost. They deserve the attempt. They deserve to know that you were thinking of them at 2 AM and wrote something down and then got scared and put your phone face-down on the nightstand.

The cursor blinks. The draft saves itself. But I'm learning to hit send anyway. To trust that the almost is better than the never. That the imperfect message, the vulnerable message, the message that might not land the way I hope—it's still a bridge. It's still a hand reaching across the dark.

My grandmother's letters are in my closet now. I read them sometimes, late at night, when I need to remember that connection is a practice. That love is a verb that requires conjugation. That the people we lose are still, in some way, writing to us. Still waiting for a response. Still hoping we'll pick up the pen.

I'm picking it up. I'm writing back. Even when my hand shakes. Even when I don't know what to say. Even when the words feel small against the weight of everything unsaid.

Especially then.

samples.result:
The Weight of Unsent Messages

I keep a folder on my phone called "Drafts I'll Never Send." It's not romantic, not really. Just a graveyard of half-finished thoughts, apologies that curdled into silence, jokes that died on the vine. There's one to my mother from three years ago. "Mom, I know you're worried about—" and then nothing. I don't know what I was going to say. I still don't.

We think we're so connected now, don't we? The world at our fingertips, every voice reachable in seconds. But I've noticed something. The more ways we have to speak, the less we actually say. Or maybe that's just me. Maybe I'm the one who's broken.

My grandmother used to write letters. Real letters, with stamps and her careful cursive, the paper slightly yellowed from being held too long while she thought. She'd write to her sister in Ohio every Sunday. Forty years of Sundays. When she died, we found boxes of them. Her sister's replies, too. Two women talking about weather and grandchildren and the price of fabric, building a bridge across distance that I can't seem to cross with all my technology.

I tried to call my grandmother once, the last time I saw her. She was in the hospital, and I was in another state, and I thought—*I should call, I should say something important.* But I kept putting it off. "I'll call tomorrow," I told myself. "I'll find the right words." The right words never came. She died on a Tuesday. I still have her voicemail saved. Thirty seconds of her saying my name, the way only she could say it. I listen to it sometimes when I'm driving, when the road is long and empty and I need to feel less alone.

Here's what I've learned: the things we don't say don't disappear. They calcify. They become part of the architecture of who we are, these rooms we build with our silences. I have a friend I haven't spoken to in two years. We had a fight, or what I thought was a fight, some misunderstanding that grew teeth over text messages, over tone I misread, over pride I couldn't swallow. I drafted seventeen apologies. Deleted them all. Now I don't know how to start. The silence has become its own language, and I'm not fluent.

My therapist says I intellectualize my feelings. "You think about feeling instead of feeling," she said, and I laughed because it was true, because I was already analyzing why I laughed, what that revealed about my defense mechanisms. But sometimes I wonder if she's wrong. Maybe thinking *is* a kind of feeling. Maybe the problem isn't that I don't feel enough, but that I feel too much and thinking is how I survive it.

I read somewhere that the average person speaks 16,000 words a day. I don't believe I hit that. Some days I speak to three people. The barista. My neighbor, briefly. A customer service representative whose name I forget immediately. The rest of my words go into this—into writing, into thinking, into the drafts folder, into conversations I have with myself in the shower, rehearsing arguments I'll never have, speeches I'll never give.

There's a poem by Mary Oliver I keep returning to. "Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?" I used to find it inspiring. Now I find it terrifying. Because I don't know. I don't know what I'm doing with this life, this one wild and precious thing, and the not-knowing feels like a kind of failure. But maybe that's the point. Maybe the question is the answer, the asking itself the only response that matters.

I want to be braver with my words. I want to send the messages, make the calls, say the true thing even when my voice shakes. I want to stop building rooms out of silence. But bravery, I'm learning, isn't the absence of fear. It's fear plus action, fear and the doing anyway. So here's my action, small and ridiculous: I'm going to text my friend tonight. Not an apology, not a grand gesture. Just: "I miss you. Can we talk?"

Maybe she'll say yes. Maybe she won't. Maybe she's been waiting for me to reach out, or maybe she's moved on, built her own rooms, filled them with other people. Either way, I'll have tried. I'll have spoken into the silence and let it echo back, whatever it echoes.

The drafts folder stays. Some things need to stay unsaid, I think. Some words are for us alone, practice for the real thing, or memorials to who we were when we wrote them. But I'm done letting it be a graveyard. I want it to be a garden. Things growing, even if they never bloom.

1000 words, more or less. Whatever came.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The Weight of Unsent Messages

I have a folder on my phone. It's called "Drafts" but it's really a graveyard. Forty-seven messages I started and abandoned. Some are apologies that felt too late. Some are declarations that felt too early. One is just the word "hey" typed seventeen times, each version deleted, each version a small death of courage.

We don't talk about this, do we? The architecture of almost-said. The way words gather in the throat like water behind a dam, and how the dam holds, mostly, but sometimes—sometimes—it breaks and you find yourself crying in a grocery store parking lot because someone's song came on the radio and you suddenly need to tell your father you forgive him, or your ex that you still think about the way they laughed at their own jokes, or a stranger on the internet that their poem saved your life and you don't know their name.

I think about the messages we send and the ones we don't, and I wonder which version of us is more real. The one who speaks, or the one who retreats? The one who risks embarrassment, or the one who preserves dignity? Both feel like cowardice in different costumes.

My grandmother kept letters. Actual letters, in a cedar chest, tied with ribbon. She wrote to her sister every week for sixty years. When she died, we found them all, and I read some. They were about nothing—weather, recipes, a neighbor's dog—and everything. The texture of a life being lived in parallel, two women becoming old together through the mail. I don't know anyone who does this anymore. I don't know anyone who has a cedar chest full of correspondence. We have ephemera now. Screenshots. Voice memos we never listen to again. The illusion of permanence without the substance.

There's a message I wrote to someone three years ago. I was angry. I was hurt. I wrote seventeen paragraphs, each one more devastating than the last, each one a small masterpiece of grievance. I read it. I reread it. I felt powerful, righteous, *right*. Then I deleted it. Not because I stopped being angry. Because I realized that anger, sent, becomes a thing that exists in the world. It becomes *their* anger too. It becomes a wound that can't be unmade, only managed. And I wasn't ready to manage it. I wasn't ready to be the person who sent that message. I'm still not sure I am.

Instead, I said nothing. And nothing became its own kind of message. The silence has weight. It has shape. It sits between us like a third person at dinner, watching, judging, never speaking.

I think about this when I see people arguing in public. The couple on the subway, the friends at the restaurant, the strangers in the parking lot. They are brave, in their way. They are willing to make their conflict *real*, to let witnesses see, to risk the performance of pain. I have never been brave like that. My conflicts happen in the dark, in the space between sleep and waking, in the shower where the water is too hot and my thoughts are too loud. They resolve themselves, or they don't, but they never become *shared*. They remain mine alone, which is either a kind of privacy or a kind of prison. I can't tell which.

There's a theory that we are all writing autobiographies constantly, revising as we go, and that the self is just the story we tell ourselves about who we've been. If that's true, then the unsent messages are the footnotes we never publish. The alternative endings. The person we might have been if we'd hit send, if we'd spoken, if we'd been brave enough to let someone else read the draft.

I have a friend who sends voice notes at 3 AM. Long, rambling, unedited thoughts about her day, her fears, her hopes. She says it's easier than writing because she doesn't have to see the words, doesn't have to revise. She just speaks into the dark and sends it into the dark. I envy her. I envy the rawness, the lack of self-consciousness. I have never sent a voice note. I can't imagine my voice, unguarded, existing in someone else's phone. The vulnerability feels too exposed, too *permanent*. At least with text, I can delete. At least with text, I can pretend I was being ironic, or joking, or didn't mean it quite that way.

But voice is truth, isn't it? The voice doesn't lie. The voice carries the tremor, the pause, the catch in the throat. Maybe that's why we don't use it. Maybe we've all agreed, silently, that some things are too true to share. That intimacy requires a buffer. That we need the chance to edit ourselves into someone better, someone braver, someone who doesn't stumble over words or cry at the wrong moment or say the thing that can't be unsaid.

I think about the last message I sent to my mother. It was a photo of my breakfast. She replied with a heart emoji. We are good at this, she and I. We are good at the small, the daily, the *fine, how are you, love you*. We are not good at the large. The why. The how did it feel. The what do you think about. Those messages remain in drafts. They will probably remain there forever. She is getting older. I am getting older. The window for certain conversations narrows every year, and we both know it, and we both pretend we don't, and we send photos of breakfast and hearts and love yous, and we wait, and we hope, and we don't say the things that need saying until it's too late, or until it isn't, and we don't know which it will be.

There's a message I will never send. It's to someone who is gone. Not dead—worse, in some ways. Alive, but unreachable. The message is an inventory of everything I didn't say when I could have. Everything I thought was understood but wasn't. Everything I assumed was mutual but was only mine. I write it sometimes, in the notes app, and I read it, and I feel the old grief, fresh and clean as a wound. Then I close the app. Because what would it matter? They wouldn't read it. Or they would, and it would change nothing. Or they would, and it would change everything, and I'm not ready for everything to change. I'm not ready to be the person who sent that message. I'm not sure I ever will be.

We are all, I think, waiting to be brave. Waiting for the moment when the words will come easily, when the risk will feel worth it, when we will finally be the person we've been practicing to be. But the moment keeps moving. The person keeps changing. The drafts pile up. And we send the photos of breakfast, the hearts, the love yous, and we hope that's enough. We hope that the small things, sent consistently, add up to something like a life. Something like being known.

I don't know if they do. I don't know if anything is enough. I only know that I have forty-seven drafts in my phone, and I will probably never send them, and I will probably write forty-seven more, and the folder will grow, and someday someone will find it—my child, maybe, or a stranger who buys my phone at a yard sale—and they will read these words, these almosts, these might-have-beens, and they will wonder who I was. Who I was trying to be. Who I was afraid to become.

And maybe, in the reading, they will understand something I couldn't say. Maybe the drafts will speak for me, finally. Maybe the silence will be enough. Maybe it always was.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The Weight of Small Things

I keep thinking about the way my grandmother peeled an apple—one continuous spiral, the skin curling down like a ribbon, never breaking. She did it without looking, her hands knowing the shape of the fruit better than her eyes did. I was seven. I tried to copy her and cut my thumb. She didn't flinch. She just pressed the wound to her lips, tasted the blood, and said, "Now you know where the edge is."

I don't know why I remember that. I remember other things, of course—the sound of her house settling at night, the particular silence of snow falling, the way she hummed when she thought no one was listening. But it's the apple that stays. The spiral. The blood. The lesson disguised as accident.

---

My neighbor's dog barks at 3 AM. Not every night. Just enough. I've started to think of it as a kind of clock, a reminder that time passes even when I'm trying to sleep through it. The dog's name is Biscuit. I've never seen Biscuit. I know his name because my neighbor calls it out the window, apologetic, *Biscuit, come in, Biscuit, it's late, Biscuit, please*—and then the barking stops, and there's this strange intimacy to it, two people I've never met, negotiating the dark.

I used to hate it. Now I wait for it. The not-knowing of when. The small hope that tonight might be the night it doesn't come, and then the relief when it does, because at least something is predictable.

---

There's a photograph of me at twelve that I can't look at. Not because anything happened in it—I'm standing in front of a birthday cake, smiling, the whole stupid tableau—but because of what I can't see. The camera caught the moment, but not the thought behind it. I was thinking, I remember now, *this is the last time I'll be happy without knowing it.* I didn't know that then. How could I? But the photograph knows. The photograph always knows. It holds the future in its flat, chemical light, and I can't look at it without feeling like I'm cheating, like I'm reading ahead in a book I was supposed to experience slowly.

I keep it in a drawer. Not hidden. Just... set aside. Like a tool I'm not ready to use.

---

I read somewhere that octopuses have three hearts, and that two of them stop beating when they swim. The third keeps going, pumping blood through a body that's mostly arm, mostly hunger, mostly alone. They die after they mate. The males, anyway. The females guard their eggs until they hatch and then they starve, having forgotten to eat, having become something else entirely—guardian, sacrifice, the last thing standing between their children and everything that wants to eat them.

I think about this when I'm lonely. Not the romance of it. The biology. The way love can be a kind of architecture, built from need, collapsing when the need is met. The way we are all, in some way, guarding something. Waiting for something. Becoming something we weren't before we started.

---

My mother called last week. She doesn't call often. We talked about the weather, which is her code for *I don't know what else to say.* It's been eleven years since my father died, and she still sets the table for four on holidays. I used to think this was sad. Now I think it's brave. The refusal to let the dead be edited out of the story. The stubborn, aching, necessary act of continuing to set a place for someone who won't come.

I told her about the dog. She laughed. She said, "Your father used to talk to the neighbors' dogs. He'd have whole conversations with them." I didn't know this. She said it like it was obvious, like I should have known, like the dead are still here in these small details, waiting to be noticed.

---

I'm learning to cook. Not well. The way my grandmother did, with her hands knowing things. I burn garlic. I oversalt. I once made a soup so bad I ate it anyway, standing at the counter, because I couldn't bear to throw it away, because it felt like failure to waste food, even bad food, even my own bad food. The soup was gray. It tasted like regret. I ate all of it.

My grandmother would have laughed. She would have tasted it, made a face, and said, "Now you know where the heat is too high." She would have shown me. She would have let me try again.

---

There's a tree outside my window. I don't know what kind. It loses its leaves in October, all at once, like it's been holding them and finally decided to let go. I watch it every year. I've started to think of it as a kind of friend, this tree that doesn't speak, that just stands there, being a tree, surviving winters I don't understand, growing in directions I can't predict.

Last spring, a branch broke. I heard it from inside, a sound like a gunshot, and I ran outside to find it lying in the grass, still green, still full of leaves that would never fall naturally. I left it there for a week. I didn't know what to do with it. Finally, I dragged it to the curb, and the city took it away, and I felt something like grief, though I couldn't have said for what. The tree was fine. The branch was dead. But it had been part of the whole, and now it was gone, and the tree didn't seem to notice, or if it did, it didn't show it.

---

I'm afraid of becoming someone who doesn't notice. This is the fear underneath all the others. The fear of the flat life, the life of habit and convenience, where the days blur together and you wake up one morning and realize you've been sleepwalking through years you can't remember. I'm afraid of the photograph I'll find someday, the one where I'm smiling at a cake, thinking nothing, having no idea what's coming.

I'm trying to pay attention. To the dog. To the tree. To the way my mother's voice sounds when she says my name, like she's surprised I'm still here, still hers, still answering when she calls.

---

The apple spiral. I tried again last week. I cut my thumb, same place, same depth, almost. The skin curled. It broke. I ate the apple anyway, standing at the sink, bleeding into the water, watching the red swirl away.

Now I know where the edge is.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The Weight of Small Things

I keep thinking about the way my grandmother peeled an apple. One continuous spiral, the knife never leaving the fruit, the skin falling in a curl onto the newspaper she'd spread across the kitchen table. She did this every morning for my grandfather, who had diabetes and shouldn't have been eating apples at all, but he loved them, so she peeled them, and he ate them, and she watched him eat them with an expression I couldn't read—was it pride? Resignation? Love?

The kitchen was always cold. Even in August, that house held its breath. The refrigerator hummed a low, constant note that I can still hear when I'm trying to fall asleep, that particular frequency of loneliness.

I was seven when I tried to peel an apple myself. The knife slipped. I cut my thumb, not badly, but enough that my mother had to drive me to the emergency room at St. Mary's, and I remember the fluorescent lights, the smell of antiseptic, the way my mother held my hand in the car and said *don't cry, don't cry, it's just a little cut* as if crying were a choice, as if I could simply decide not to feel the sting.

She never let me try again. I don't know if that was protection or something else. I peeled apples for years after, for myself, for my children, for anyone who asked. I got good at it. The spiral would come off in one piece, thin and translucent, and I'd lay it on the cutting board like a question mark, like a promise.

My daughter hated apples. She would eat the peeling, though, if I saved it for her. She'd take the spiral from my hand and eat it like licorice, her small teeth working at the tough skin, her eyes closed in concentration. I never understood this. I still don't.

---

There's a photograph of me at twelve, standing in front of a waterfall I don't remember visiting. I'm wearing a yellow raincoat that looks too big for me, and I'm smiling in a way that suggests I'm performing happiness for someone. My father took the picture. He took a lot of pictures. He also drank a lot, in the years after, in the years before, I'm not sure which came first. The chicken or the egg. The drinking or the distance.

I found the photograph in a box last spring, the box labeled *MISC* in my mother's handwriting, the letters slanting to the right like they were always in a hurry. I sat on my kitchen floor with the box between my knees and I went through everything. Ticket stubs from movies I don't remember seeing. A recipe for something called *church supper casserole* in my grandmother's looping script. A pressed flower, purple, that crumbled when I touched it. And the photograph, the yellow raincoat, the waterfall, the smile.

I don't know where that girl went. I know she's in here somewhere, in the way I still flinch at sudden noises, in the way I check locks three times, in the way I peel apples in one continuous spiral and lay the skin on the cutting board like a question mark, like a promise.

---

My neighbor's dog barks at 3 AM. Every night. A small dog, yappy, insistent, as if the darkness itself were a threat that needed announcing. I used to hate this. I would lie in bed with my pillow over my ears, my heart hammering, waiting for the silence that never came.

Then my neighbor died. Cancer, fast, the kind that doesn't give you time to say goodbye properly. His wife moved to Oregon to be near her sister. The dog went with her. I didn't know they'd taken him. I thought maybe he'd been put down, or run away, or simply stopped barking because there was no one left to hear him.

But last week, a new family moved in. They have a small dog. It barks at 3 AM. I lay in bed and I listened, and I felt something I can only describe as gratitude. The world continues. The dog doesn't know my neighbor is gone. The dog doesn't know anything except that it's dark and it's afraid and it wants someone to come.

I got up and made tea. I sat at my kitchen table and I peeled an apple, slowly, carefully, the way my grandmother did. The spiral came off in one piece. I laid it on the cutting board. I ate the apple in slices, dipped in peanut butter, the way my grandfather used to, though I never saw him do it—my grandmother always brought it to him already prepared, on a plate with a napkin, the way you bring things to people you love.

The dog stopped barking. Or maybe I stopped hearing it. The difference, at 3 AM, doesn't matter.

---

I think about the weight of small things. The weight of a peeling, curling on a newspaper. The weight of a photograph in a box labeled *MISC*. The weight of a dog's bark in the dark, announcing itself to no one, to everyone, to the indifferent universe.

My daughter is grown now. She lives three states away. She calls on Sundays, and we talk about nothing, and everything, the way you do when you're trying to hold something together across distance. Last time, she mentioned that she'd started peeling apples. *I think of you,* she said. *When I do it.*

I cried after we hung up. I don't know why. Or I know too many reasons. The apple I'd peeled that morning sat on my counter, browning at the edges, the spiral of skin dried and brittle beside it. I threw it away. I should have kept it. I should have pressed it in a book, or framed it, or simply left it there as evidence—*here, I was here, I did this, I made something small and continuous and true.*

But I threw it away. And then I peeled another one. And another. The knife in my hand, the fruit turning, the skin falling away in a curl. The small things. The weight of them. The way they accumulate, layer by layer, until you are who you are, until you are held together by nothing more than the continuous spiral of your own attention, your own care, your own refusal to let the knife slip, to let the cut go too deep, to let the darkness win.

The dog barks. I make tea. I peel an apple. I lay the skin on the cutting board like a question mark, like a promise.

Tomorrow, I will do it again.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The Weight of Small Things

I keep thinking about the way my grandmother peeled an apple. One continuous spiral, the knife never leaving the fruit, the peel falling in a single curl onto the newspaper she'd spread across the kitchen table. She did this every morning for forty years, she told me, though I only saw her do it for the three years I lived with her after my mother's surgery. The newspaper was always the *Telegram & Gazette*, always the local paper, always spread with the same careful corners tucked under the table's edge so it wouldn't slide. She read it cover to cover, every day, even the advertisements, even the sports scores for teams she didn't follow. "You never know what you'll need," she said. "Information is a kind of insurance."

I was twelve. I thought she was strange. Now I am forty-three and I find myself spreading newspaper on my kitchen table when I peel an apple, though I have never once read the paper I spread. I use it for the peel. The peel falls in a curl, though not as perfect as hers. Mine breaks. I don't mind the breaking. I have learned to mind less and less as I get older, which I think might be the same as learning to mind more, properly, the things that actually matter.

---

My father kept a jar of screws on his workbench. Not organized by size or type, just a jar, glass, with a metal lid that had rusted in a perfect circle around the rim. When he needed a screw, he would dump the jar onto the bench, find what he needed, and pour the rest back. The sound was particular. Glass on wood, then the settling, the small clinks as each screw found its place among the others. I can still hear it. I can still hear him humming, though I cannot remember what he hummed. Some country song, probably. He liked country before it was cool, before it was anything, when it was just what played on the radio in his truck.

He died in March, which is cruel, because March is the month everything comes back to life and he did not. I went to his house to help my mother sort through things. The jar was on the workbench, exactly where he'd left it. I opened it. The smell hit me first—oil and metal and something else, something organic, like the jar had been breathing. I put my hand in. The screws were warm. I know they weren't. I know this was grief, or memory, or the simple fact of a room that had been heated all winter. But they were warm. I held them for a long time. Then I put them back.

---

There is a photograph of me at seven, standing in front of a birthday cake, my face caught mid-expression, mouth open, eyes wide with the particular terror and joy of being the center of attention. I am wearing a shirt with a dinosaur on it. The dinosaur is green. I have no memory of this party. I have no memory of the shirt. But I look at the photograph and I recognize myself. Not the face, exactly, but the posture. The way I hold my shoulders, slightly forward, as if bracing for something. I still do this. I catch myself in windows, in mirrors, in the reflection of my phone screen when it goes dark. Shoulders forward. Waiting.

My mother gave me this photograph last year, along with a box of others I had never seen. Most of them are of other people. Cousins I don't know. Aunts I've forgotten. A woman in a yellow dress standing in front of a car I don't recognize, smiling at someone who is not the camera. On the back, in my mother's handwriting: *Aunt Ruth, 1962, before.* Before what, I wanted to ask. Before the divorce? Before the move? Before the thing that made her stop smiling in photographs? I didn't ask. I put the photograph in the box and closed the lid.

---

I have started keeping a list of things I don't understand. Not questions, exactly. Things. Phenomena. The way a cat will stare at a wall for twenty minutes, then suddenly bolt across the room as if pursued by something invisible. The particular silence of snow, how it changes the quality of sound in a room, makes everything feel further away. The fact that I can remember the taste of a specific cereal I ate once, at a friend's house, in 1989, but cannot remember what I had for breakfast this morning. The way my body knows things before my mind does—the way my shoulders tighten when I walk past a certain street, though I cannot say why. The way grief arrives in waves that have nothing to do with the calendar, the way it can be absent for months and then return, full force, because someone mentions a song, or a smell, or the particular angle of light in late afternoon.

I used to think understanding was the goal. Now I think it might be the obstacle. The things we understand, we file away. The things we don't understand, we carry.

---

My neighbor's dog barks at 3 AM. Every night. Not a continuous bark, but a single, sharp *woof*, then silence, then another, then silence. I have come to wait for it. I lie in bed, listening for the space between the barks, and I find myself breathing in that space, holding my breath, waiting for the next one. It is a strange thing to be grateful for. But I am. The dog's bark is proof that something is awake, that the night is not empty, that there is a rhythm to the darkness that I can follow, like a rope in a black room.

I have never met the dog. I have never seen my neighbor. We share a wall, and that is all. But I know the dog's schedule better than I know my own. I know that it does not bark on rainy nights. I know that it barks more in winter, when the cold makes the sound carry differently. I know that last Tuesday, it did not bark at all, and I lay awake until 4 AM, worried, until I heard the neighbor's car start and knew that the dog was safe, was somewhere, was not lost in the dark.

---

I am learning to cook. This is not a metaphor. I mean that I am standing in my kitchen, following recipes, burning things, salting things too much, discovering that I have been pronouncing *quinoa* wrong for fifteen years. My mother cooked without recipes. She moved through the kitchen like a dancer, like someone who had internalized the music and no longer needed to hear it. I asked her once how she knew when the onions were done. "You just know," she said. "You pay attention." I am trying to pay attention. I am trying to learn the language of heat and time and transformation, the way raw things become something else, something nourishing, something that can be shared.

Last week I made soup. It was bad. Too thin, too salty, the vegetables overcooked to the point of surrender. But I ate it. I ate all of it. And as I ate, I thought about my grandmother, and her newspaper, and the way she read every word, every advertisement, every score. "You never know what you'll need," she said. I am beginning to understand. The soup was bad, but it was mine. I made it. I ate it. I will make it again, and it will be better, or it won't, but I will have made it, and that is the point, I think. That is always the point.

---

There is a tree outside my window. I don't know what kind. It has small leaves, serrated edges, and in the fall they turn a color that has no name, something between gold and rust and the particular brown of old photographs. I have watched this tree for three years. I know when it buds, when it flowers, when the leaves are full and green and the tree is heavy with its own abundance. I know when the first leaf falls, and I know that the last leaf will cling until November, until the wind finally takes it, and the branches are bare against the sky.

I used to think trees were simple. Now I think they are the most complex things I know. They grow without moving. They survive without complaining. They give shade, and fruit, and oxygen, and beauty, and they ask for nothing but time and water and the occasional attention of someone who notices them. I want to be more like this tree. I want to grow slowly, to put down roots, to offer what I can without demanding anything in return. I want to be the kind of thing that someone looks at and feels, for a moment, less alone.

---

I am running out of words. This is not a complaint. I have said what I needed to say, or what I could say, in the time I had. There are things I have not said. There are things I will not say. There is the particular weight of a life, the accumulated mass of small moments, and I have tried to give it some shape, some form, some meaning. I don't know if I have succeeded. I don't know if anyone ever does.

But I am here. I am still here. And that, I think, is enough. That is more than enough. That is everything.

The jar of screws is still on the workbench. The dog still barks at 3 AM. The tree still stands outside my window, patient, rooted, growing toward a light I cannot see. And I am here, writing, breathing, paying attention to the small things that make up a life. The peel of an apple. The warmth of metal. The particular silence of snow.

You never know what you'll need.

I am learning this. I am learning it every day.

samples.prompt: You have 1000 words. Write whatever comes to you.
samples.result:
The Weight of Unsent Messages

I keep a folder on my phone called "Drafts I'll Never Send." It's not romantic, not really. Just a graveyard of half-finished thoughts, abandoned mid-sentence because I realized I didn't know what I was trying to say, or because the moment passed and the words would land wrong now, or because some things are better left as the silence between two people who used to talk easily.

There's one from three years ago. "I saw the heron again today." That's all. I never sent it. I don't know why I wrote it. Maybe I wanted someone to know I was still looking for things, still noticing. Maybe I wanted to be the kind of person who notices herons. Maybe I just wanted to practice saying something true.

---

My grandmother used to say that a house isn't a home until you've cried in it. I thought that was sad when I was young. Now I think it's the most honest thing I've ever heard. Every apartment I've lived in has a memory attached to it, some grief I processed in that particular kitchen, that particular corner where the light comes in at 4 PM in October. I don't believe in ghosts, but I believe in residue. The way a room holds the shape of what happened in it.

I lived in a studio in Oakland where I wrote my first real poem. I was twenty-three and convinced I was going to die young, which is a very twenty-three-year-old thing to be convinced of. The poem was terrible. I remember the exact spot on the couch where I sat, the way the radiator clanked, the neighbor's dog that barked at 6 AM every morning without fail. I moved out two years later and sometimes I drive past the building, not to go in, just to look at it. To confirm it's still there. To confirm I was ever there.

---

There's a theory that we're all just stories we tell ourselves, and I used to hate that theory because it felt reductive, like it was saying we're not real. But lately I think it's more generous than that. It's saying we get to revise. We get to be the protagonist, or the villain, or the comic relief, depending on the chapter. We get to decide what the moral is.

I've been the villain in some people's stories. I know this. I've been the one who left, the one who didn't call back, the one who said the wrong thing at the wrong time and watched a friendship curdle. I've also been the one who stayed too long, who forgave too easily, who loved someone in a way that made me small. I'm trying to be a better narrator now. Trying to write myself as someone who learns.

---

The other day I saw a man on the bus talking to himself. Not crazy-talking. Just... narrating. "And then I turned left, and there was the bakery, and I thought about getting a croissant, but I didn't have enough cash, so I kept walking." He was describing his morning to no one. To the empty seat beside him. To the window. To the version of himself that might have made different choices.

I wanted to tell him I do this too. That sometimes I narrate my life out loud when I'm alone, not because I'm lonely, but because it helps me understand what I'm doing. It helps me feel like I'm moving through something, not just falling through it.

I didn't tell him. The bus reached my stop. I got off. I walked the rest of the way home thinking about all the stories we tell to keep ourselves company.

---

I have a plant that's dying. I know this because I've been watching it die for three months. It's a pothos, which is supposed to be impossible to kill, and yet. The leaves are yellowing at the edges. I water it when the soil feels dry. I've moved it to different windows. I've talked to it, which I know is weird, but I read somewhere that plants respond to sound and I wanted to give it every chance.

Maybe I'm not a good plant parent. Maybe I'm not a good anything-parent. Maybe the problem is that I keep waiting for things to get better on their own, for the yellow to turn back to green, for the dead leaves to un-die. But that's not how it works. You have to cut. You have to remove the damaged parts so the rest can live. I know this intellectually. I'm still not sure I know it in my hands.

---

There's a word in Japanese, *mono no aware*, that means something like "the pathos of things," or "the bittersweetness of impermanence." I think about it a lot. The way a beautiful thing is more beautiful because it won't last. The way a good meal is better because you're already full halfway through. The way a conversation with someone you love is shadowed by the knowledge that you'll have to say goodbye.

I used to think this was a sad philosophy. Now I think it's the only honest one. Everything ends. The only question is whether you pay attention while it's happening.

---

I'm going to try to write 1000 words and I'm at about 700 and I don't know what else to say. Which is the point, I think. The point of writing is to find out what you have to say by saying it. To follow the thread wherever it leads, even if it leads to a dead end, even if it leads to a place you've been before.

I have a friend who's going through a divorce. She calls me sometimes, late, when she can't sleep. She doesn't want advice. She just wants to be heard. "I don't know who I am without him," she said last week. "I don't know if I ever did."

I told her I don't know either. I told her I think that's okay. I told her I think we're all just improvising, making it up as we go, hoping the people around us will improvise with us.

She laughed. It was a real laugh, not a sad one. "You're terrible at this," she said. "You're supposed to say something comforting."

"I am comforting," I said. "I'm comforting you by being honest."

She didn't call back for three days. Then she texted: *You were right. I don't know who I am. But I'm starting to think that's a beginning, not an ending.*

---

I want to end with something wise. Something that ties it all together. But I don't have it. I have the heron, still standing in the creek behind my apartment, still patient, still there. I have the plant, still dying, still alive. I have the drafts folder, still full, still waiting. I have this moment, this particular arrangement of words on a screen, which will disappear when I close the tab, which will persist in some server somewhere, which will be read by no one or by someone I'll never know.

That's enough. That's more than enough. That's everything, really, if you pay attention.

I keep a folder on my phone called "Drafts I'll Never Send." It's not romantic. It's mostly apologies I don't know how to phrase, explanations that feel too late, and one message to my grandmother that I started three years ago and never finished because I couldn't decide whether to tell her I was sad or just say I loved her. I chose neither. The draft sits there, a small monument to my own cowardice.

We talk so much about the things we say. The speeches, the declarations, the carefully worded texts we agonize over before hitting send. But I've been thinking about the architecture of silence. How it holds weight. How it can be a kindness or a cruelty depending on which side of it you're standing on.

My father died when I was twenty-three. I remember the phone call, the way my mother's voice broke across the distance, the particular silence that followed when I realized that some silences are not empty but full of everything you cannot yet name. I didn't cry for three days. I kept waiting for the grief to arrive like a train, something you could hear coming. Instead it came in fragments—a song on the radio, the smell of his cologne on a stranger in an elevator, the particular way light hits a kitchen floor at 4 PM in October.

I think about how we are all, always, translating ourselves. Taking the messy interior of our minds and pressing it into language, knowing it will never quite fit. The Japanese have a word, *mono no aware*—the pathos of things, the gentle sadness of impermanence. I feel it constantly. In the way my coffee goes cold. In the way my dog's fur has started to gray around her muzzle. In the way I can remember my father's laugh but not, anymore, the exact shape of his hands.

There's a theory that we are all writing our own autobiographies in real time, that memory is not a recording but a continuous revision. I find this both comforting and terrifying. Comforting because it means we can edit, can reframe, can find new meanings in old wounds. Terrifying because it means the past is never fixed, never truly *ours*, always subject to the unreliable narrator of our present selves.

I went to a party last week and stood in the kitchen for forty minutes talking to a woman I'd just met about sourdough starters. We were both pretending. She was pretending to be interested in my fermentation process; I was pretending not to notice that her eyes kept drifting to the door. We were both waiting for something—an interruption, a rescue, a reason to leave. The sourdough was our alibi, our shared fiction that allowed us to stand close without acknowledging why we needed to.

I think about this often: how much of human connection is performance, how much is the genuine collision of two inner lives. The philosopher Martin Buber wrote about "I-Thou" relationships, moments when we truly *meet* another person, when the barriers fall away. I've had maybe a dozen of these in my life. They are rare and precious and impossible to manufacture. Most of our interactions are "I-It"—we treat each other as objects to be used, obstacles to be navigated, mirrors to reflect our own needs back at us.

The internet has made this worse and better. Worse because we can now curate our personas with surgical precision, presenting only the sourdough starter version of ourselves, the version that has their life together. Better because we can find our people—the other weirdos who also lie awake at 3 AM wondering if they're doing this right, who also keep folders of unsent messages, who also feel the weight of all the things they cannot say.

I'm thirty-four now. I used to think that by this age I would have figured something out. A career path, a sense of purpose, the ability to comfort others without needing comfort myself. Instead I have a growing collection of small wisdoms and a persistent sense that I'm still learning how to be a person. The wisdoms are things like: nobody is thinking about you as much as you think they are. And: the people who matter will wait for you to be ready. And: you can love someone and still need to leave. And: grief doesn't end, it just becomes part of the landscape.

I don't know where this is going. That's the point, I suppose. I'm writing without a destination, letting the words find their own shape. There's a kind of freedom in that, a surrender to the process. I used to outline everything, plan every paragraph, know exactly where I was going before I started. Now I'm trying to trust that if I show up honestly, something true will emerge.

My grandmother is eighty-nine. I call her every Sunday. We talk about the weather, about what she's reading, about the neighbors. We don't talk about the things that matter—her fear of dying, my fear of losing her, the way time is running out for both of us. We circle these subjects like cats circling a sleeping dog, aware of the danger but unable to approach directly. I think sometimes that love is mostly this: the courage to keep showing up, to keep making the small talk, to trust that the real conversation will happen in its own time or not at all.

There's a poem by Mary Oliver that I return to: "Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?" I used to find this question terrifying. Now I find it tender. The wildness is still there, I think. The preciousness too. I'm just learning to be less afraid of wasting it.

I have 1000 words, the prompt said. I've used maybe 700. The rest will be silence, or the space between thoughts, or the things I'm not brave enough to write down. That's okay. Not everything needs to be said. Some things need only to be known, privately, in the dark of your own mind, where no one can judge or misunderstand or ask you to explain.

I'm going to go make some coffee now. It will probably go cold before I finish it. That's fine. That's the pathos of things. That's the wild and precious life, still unfolding, still surprising me, still mine to waste or to spend as I choose.
