The Weight of Unsent Messages

I have a folder on my phone called "Drafts" that terrifies me. Not because of what's in it—mostly half-finished grocery lists and a recipe for soup I'll never make—but because of what it represents. The space where words go to almost happen. The liminal zone between intention and action.

My grandmother used to say that a letter written but never sent still carries its weight. She kept every letter she ever received, even the ones from people she'd stopped speaking to, even the angry ones, even the ones that arrived too late. "Paper remembers," she'd say, though she couldn't have explained what she meant. I think she meant that once something is written down, it exists somewhere, even if no one reads it. The universe has been notified. Something has shifted.

I think about this when I don't text someone back. When I type "Hey, how are you" and delete it. When I compose an entire apology in my head at 2 AM and wake up to find I never opened the messaging app. The words exist in some quantum state, I suppose. Potential energy. The possibility of connection, hovering.

There's a particular loneliness to being surrounded by people you could reach out to. My phone knows 847 contacts. I have spoken to perhaps forty of them in the past year. The rest are ghosts I carry around, names and faces that surface when I'm scrolling, triggering some memory of warmth or conflict or simple coexistence. I used to feel guilty about this. Now I think it's just the human condition, amplified. We were never meant to maintain hundreds of relationships. We were meant for villages, for tribes, for knowing everyone's children and dogs and ailments. The modern world asks us to perform intimacy at scale, and we fail, and we feel bad about failing, and the feeling bad becomes its own kind of isolation.

I met a man once who claimed he could remember every conversation he'd ever had. Not the gist—the actual words, the order, the pauses. He was a trial lawyer, which explained the skill but not the curse. He said it made him unbearable at parties. People would say something casual, and he'd correct them. "No, you said 'I think' not 'I feel,' and you looked at the ceiling, and there was a seventeen-second silence before you laughed." He was lonely in a very specific way. He knew too much about how little we mean when we speak. The performance of conversation, the scripts we run, the ways we edit ourselves in real-time. He could see all of it, and it made genuine connection nearly impossible. He wanted to be known, but he couldn't stop seeing the machinery of being known.

I think about him when I read old journals. The person I was at twenty-three, at nineteen, at thirty-one. The earnestness, the suffering, the absolute certainty that this particular heartbreak or triumph would define everything. I want to reach back and tell her something. But what? That it gets better? That it gets worse? That the categories themselves dissolve, that the person she's becoming isn't better or worse, just more accumulated, more sedimentary, layers of experience pressing down into something that might, if she's lucky, resemble wisdom?

My mother has dementia now. Or had—it's progressed to the point where "has" feels like the wrong verb, like she's moved into a different tense entirely. She lives in a facility. When I visit, she sometimes knows me. Sometimes she thinks I'm her sister, dead for thirty years. Sometimes she's a child herself, frightened by the unfamiliar room. The woman who raised me, who taught me to read, who could recite poetry from memory, who once drove three hours in a snowstorm because I had a fever—she's still there, somewhere, but I can't reliably find her. I talk to her anyway. I tell her about my day, about the weather, about things she wouldn't care about. I hold her hand. She holds mine back, sometimes, with a grip that surprises me with its strength.

This is what unsent messages become, eventually. Not drafts in a folder, but words spoken into absence. The practice of love when love can no longer be received in the form we offer it. I don't know if she hears me. I don't know if it matters. I know that I need to speak, that the speaking is its own kind of keeping, that something in the air shifts when we name our love out loud, even to empty rooms.

There's a theory that consciousness is fundamental to the universe, not emergent from it. That matter is what consciousness looks like from the outside. I don't know if it's true. I like that it's possible. It would mean that my unsent messages exist somewhere, that the potential for connection is a kind of reality, that the universe is listening even when no one is.

I used to believe in a God who read everything, who knew the secrets we kept even from ourselves. I don't believe that anymore, or not in that way. But I haven't lost the habit of confession. Of speaking into the dark and hoping, against evidence, that something is there. The habit itself is a kind of faith. The willingness to be vulnerable in the absence of guarantee.

I'm going to send a message now. To someone I haven't spoken to in months. Not an apology, not an explanation. Just: I was thinking of you. I hope you're well. The simplest possible thing. The thing I've been drafting for weeks.

The send button is a small violence. The irreversible commitment of words to the world. Once it's done, it's done. No more editing, no more second-guessing, no more the comfort of potential. Only consequence.

I press it.

The message is delivered. Read, eventually. A response comes: "You too. Miss you."

And just like that, the ghost becomes a person again. The folder in my phone grows smaller by one. The weight shifts, redistributes, finds a new equilibrium.

This is what I have. The thousand words and the one that mattered. The practice of reaching, the risk of being reached back. The endless, necessary work of trying to be known, and of knowing, in a world that makes it so difficult and so essential.

I'll write again tomorrow. I'll send something. I'll hold my mother's hand and tell her about the soup I didn't make, the recipe I never tried, the life that continues in all its unfinished forms.

The drafts folder will fill again. The ghosts will gather. And I will keep speaking, because what else is there to do, in the end, but to keep speaking?
